title: Sony Wins Rights In Host Of International Territories To A24’s ‘You Can See Everything’ & ‘Primetime’
full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News Dan Lin Is Out As Film Boss At Netflix Read the full story By Andreas Wiseman Andreas Wiseman Executive Editor, Film & International @AndreasWiseman More Stories By Andreas Cineverse Wins North American Rights To Thriller-Horror ‘The Night Driver’ With Josh Lucas, Alyssa Milano & David Arquette Indonesian Star & ‘Reacher’ Actress Agnez Mo Joins Nicolas Cage & Michael Sheen In Cyber-Thriller ‘C.L.A.Y.’ Daylight Adds Deuxmoi Podcast Deux U To Network View All October 19, 2026 9:16am Add us as a Google Preferred Source 'You Can See Everything' and 'Primetime' A24 EXCLUSIVE : In a competitive situation, Sony Pictures Worldwide Acquisitions has acquired rights in a host of international markets to A24 ’s awards season movies You Can See Everything and Primetime . Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s Elizabeth Holmes doc You Can See Everything made its North American debut this weekend with a historic opening, ranking among the largest limited-release openings of the century and marking the biggest documentary opening in more than 20 years. The film, a mind-bending fly on the wall doc in which Theranos founder Holmes invites Fielder and Oppenheim into her home before she is sent to prison, has scored sky high ratings on Letterboxd, Rotten Tomatoes and Metacritic. Related Stories News Jesse Eisenberg TV Series Produced By Peter Rice To Be Taken Out By A24 News How A24 Spurred A Meme Craze & Got The Many To Watch 'You Can See Everything'; Documentary Opens To $15M Milestone Sony Pictures has picked up rights in Germany & Austria, Latin America, Scandinavia, Greece, the Middle East, Israel, India, South Africa, South Korea, and Southeast Asia. Watch on Deadline Directed by Lance Oppenheim, Venice drama Primetime is currently playing in North American theaters and select international markets, where it has grossed more than $50M to date. Robert Pattinson stars as Chris Hansen, the Dateline NBC journalist who hosted controversial but popular show To Catch a Predator . Sony Pictures has taken rights for Primetime in Middle East, Indonesia, Israel, Singapore, Switzerland, South Korea, South Africa, Thailand, and Vietnam, with theatrical releases currently being planned across those regions. The deals reunite Sony Pictures Worldwide Acquisitions with A24 following Materialists , which earned north of $70M internationally for Sony Pictures and brought the film’s worldwide total past $100M. The A24 deal was negotiated on behalf of the studio by Joe Matukewicz, President, Sony Pictures Worldwide Acquisitions; Virginia Longmuir, EVP, Business Affairs; and Elan Kovo, VP, Business Development & FP&A. title: Egyptian Star Mona Zaki Reflects on Three Decades of Reinvention as El Gouna Honors Her Career: ‘Art Is About Freedom’
full_text: Oct 19, 2026 9:00am PT Egyptian Star Mona Zaki Reflects on Three Decades of Reinvention as El Gouna Honors Her Career: ‘Art Is About Freedom’ By Essie Assibu Plus Icon Essie Assibu Latest 10 Films to Track at El Gouna, From Cannes and Berlin Standouts to Rising Arab Filmmakers 3 days ago El Gouna’s Amr Mansi on CineGouna Expansion, New Partnerships and Making ‘the Industry Our Hero’ 3 days ago El Gouna Artistic Director Andrew Mohsen Puts ‘Discovery’ First: ‘We’re Trying to Draw Attention’ to Overlooked Films 3 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Courtesy of Alia Rady The 9th edition of El Gouna Film Festival (Oct. 15-23) may be celebrating Mona Zaki ’s past, but the Egyptian film star is far more interested in what she’s yet to do. Honored with the festival’s Career Achievement Award at the opening ceremony, Zaki, who has already built a career spanning more than three decades, hasn’t even turned 50. Sitting down with Variety on the shores of the Red Sea, she speaks about that prolific career less as a completed body of work than a continuous process of reinvention. That ongoing transformation has required her to repeatedly shed audiences’ expectations of who Mona Zaki should be. “I get bored easily with myself,” she shares. Related Stories Taylor Swift's 'Patient Zero' Bumps 'Choosin' Texas' Out of No. 1 on Hot 100; 'Encore' Tracks Fill Four Out of Five Top Slots Taylor Swift's 'Patient Zero' Holds Steady at No. 1 for Second Week on Singles Chart Looking back, Zaki says two lessons in particular stand out: learning the power of saying “no” and finding the confidence and willingness to express herself, both personally and emotionally. The latter, she confides, was something acting itself helped teach her. Popular on Variety “You just have to open up,” she reflects. “Your emotions are important to be heard, and it’s okay. Part of your healing is saying what you feel.” Zaki entered the industry young, first in theater, before moving into television and, ultimately, the silver screen. Early on, she became closely associated with the “girl next door,” an image that increasingly felt at odds with both the woman she was becoming and the kinds of characters she wanted to explore. “I started to kind of feel like I’m going there doing the same thing in every different project,” she recalls. “How boring is that? I needed to shift.” That turning point came with Yousry Nasrallah’s 2009 drama “ Scheherazade, Tell Me a Story ” (Ehky Ya Shahrazad), written by the late Wahid Hamed, which saw Zaki take on the role of a television host whose program examines the experiences of women navigating romance, health, everyday life, and the expectations placed upon them by Egyptian society. The departure from Zaki’s familiar screen persona drew intense backlash, with audiences questioning what had happened to the “girl next door” they had come to know. The response shook her enough that she turned to Hamed with concerns about facing the film’s promotional tour. He encouraged her to stand behind a choice she had made out of love for the work, advice that helped Zaki confront the resistance to seeing her move beyond the roles that had defined her early career. For Zaki, the experience marked the beginning of a struggle that has followed her throughout her career, that of finding roles that allow women to address subjects Egyptian cinema has historically treated as difficult or off-limits. “Censorship, talking about taboos, things that are not okay most of the time, especially for women to talk about,” remain among the challenges she continues to face. “I’m still living in that struggle even now. It can be very difficult to find a meaningful script.” While she believes the landscape has advanced over more than 30 years, Zaki remains deeply frustrated by the gap between the talent of Egypt’s actresses and the opportunities afforded them. “It breaks my heart that most of them are not taking the chances they deserve and the topics they would love to talk about and the rights they want to stand for.” Her own connection with audiences is something she has learned to negotiate over time. “It’s a relationship. You work on it like any other relationship in your life,” she explains. Part of that relationship, she believes, means establishing boundaries around her freedom to evolve as an artist. “I have the right not to feel bored and sick of myself doing the same thing because I’m not corporate, I’m an artist,” she stresses. “Art is about freedom, it’s about change, it’s about trial and error.” With each role, Zaki starts by building a life for the character beyond what exists in the script. She works with an acting coach on every project, drawing on different techniques to construct the character’s history. One of the most important parts of that process, she explains, is imagining a character’s life before the audience ever meets her. Zaki might close her eyes and picture the woman she’s playing at seven years old, in her childhood home with her mother, building memories and emotional associations that will never appear on screen but are critical to the performance. “I don’t have to say it, but I can make people feel it the way I felt it.” That method was put to a different test with “ El Sett ,” Marwan Hamed’s biopic of Umm Kulthum. This time, Zaki was building a character from the life of one of the Arab world’s most revered cultural figures, with decades of history and public memory with which to contend. She plunged into what she calls “crazy research,” watching every piece of footage she could find and repeatedly listening to a rare two-hour radio interview that became one of her most important references. “The whole internal emotions are the imagination of the writer and me.” While the facts of Umm Kulthum’s life are immutable, Zaki still had to find the woman behind them. To bridge that gap, Zaki imagined the parts of Kulthum’s life no archive could relate: the emotions, relationships and private struggles that might have shaped her from childhood. The character stayed with Zaki long after cameras stopped rolling, and she found it difficult to sever that connection after filming wrapped. “I came out of the project feeling that I’m a 70-year-old woman. I’m serious, this was not a joke.” For months, she had taken on not only the physical transformation into Kulthum, but also the emotions and experiences of a woman decades older than herself. Fully returning to Mona Zaki proved disorienting. “I think my whole face changed after that,” she recalls. “I couldn’t accept myself in the mirror.” Some of Kulthum has proven difficult to shake. “I’m trying to get rid of her,” Zaki muses. “I only have a few leftovers, gladly. Honestly, I don’t want to feel like I’m 70 and I’m not there yet.” Asked what she looks for in a role now, after more than three decades of acting, Zaki doesn’t hesitate. “Reality. Honesty. title: Ticketmaster Goes All-In on AI, Names Ex-Amazon Exec as Chief Technology Officer
full_text: Oct 19, 2026 9:00am PT Ticketmaster Goes All-In on AI, Names Ex-Amazon Exec as Chief Technology Officer By Corbin Bolies Plus Icon Corbin Bolies Latest Anna Faris Says ‘It Hurts’ After ‘Mom’ Creator Chuck Lorre Admits His ‘Reluctance to Hire’ Her Was Proven ‘Correct’ After She Exited the Show 3 days ago CNN and Google Strike Multiyear Partnership to Embrace Generative AI 4 days ago Trump Says Execution of Fort Hood Shooter by Firing Squad Will Not Be Livestreamed 4 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Courtesy of Ticketmaster Bot attacks have plagued Ticketmaster for years, so to combat it, the ticketing service is shaking up its executive ranks and going all-in on AI. Ticketmaster has hired Jim Freeman as its chief technology officer, filling a slot left vacant since February after its London-based chief technology officer, Carlos Alvarez-Coch, departed ahead of a deposition in the U.S. government’s antitrust trial against parent company Live Nation. It has also appointed Rachel Smith, a veteran of Block (owner of music service Tidal), to be its first senior vice president of data science and machine learning, and Disney and Stripe product veteran Chuck Mortimore as its next senior vice president of product. Related Stories Todd Rundgren Slams Taylor Swift, Says She ‘Ruined Music’ and Is ‘the Apotheosis of Mediocrity’ Taylor Swift's 'Encore' Edition Boosts 'The Life of a Showgirl' Back to No. 1 for First Time Since January, Adding a 13th Week on Top As part of the AI push, Ticketmaster has also brought on the team from Raige.ai, an AI startup the company acquired in July. The team will boost Ticketmaster’s adoption of AI tools across the company while also building out the platform’s AI infrastructure. Popular on Variety “Reliable, secure and personalized experiences depend on how effectively we use technology and data,” Saumil Mehta, Ticketmaster’s global president, said in a statement. “Jim, Rachel, Chuck and the Ragie.ai team will help us move faster, build better tools and deliver better outcomes for fans, artists, venues and clients.” Freeman’s remit as chief technology officer will tackle all things AI: building AI tools, using the technology to power fan experiences and ensuring its adoption across Ticketmaster’s organization. Freeman joined the company after a stint as senior adviser at Permira, though he formerly worked as a vice president at Amazon to build and launch Prime Video and its respective device and distribution partnerships. Smith’s work will include an expanded focus on data science and analytics, including tightening integration between data and the company’s broader product development, while Mortimore will help lead product strategy to help combat the company’s bot issues and ensure fans have easier access to both their accounts and their tickets. Gomez-Rejon will also direct the second episode and will serve as executive producer of the episodes. Based on the bestselling comic book series by Roberto Aguirre-Sacasa and Francesco Francavilla, Afterlife with Archie turns the all-American town of Riverdale into a zombie-overrun apocalypse — where the only thing scarier than the undead is trying to survive your teenage years. When a supernatural spell from a certain teen witch backfires, unleashing an army of the possessed dead upon Riverdale, Archie and his friends must fight to stay alive, testing the friendships, romances and loyalties that have always held them together. Additional credits include the Benedict Cumberbatch film The Current War . Gomez-Rejon also received an Outstanding Directing for a Miniseries or Movie Emmy nomination for American Horror Story: Coven . The director currently has work lined up on the Apple TV series Stowaway, starring Oscar Isaac as Juan Carlos Guzmán; the film The Fortress of Solitude ; and the TV adaptation of Edna Ferber’s book Giant at Amazon. It delves into the psyche of a torrid romance and subsequent act of murder between two young, adulterous but God-fearing lovers — believed to be played by Garner and Pullman — unraveling their complex lives and the emotional toll of living as killers for 18 years. title: Foo Fighters, Weezer, Sublime Join KROQ’s 2026 Almost Acoustic Christmas Lineup
full_text: × Skip to main content Breaking News Netflix Film Head Dan Lin Out close By Kimberly Nordyke Plus Icon Kimberly Nordyke Managing Editor, Digital View All October 19, 2026 8:55am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Dave Grohl of Foo Fighters. Daniel Boczarski/Getty Images for Harley-Davidson Foo Fighters , Weezer and Sublime are among the recording acts that will be on the lineup for this year’s KROQ Almost Acoustic Christmas. Interpol, Joyce Manor, Julia Wolf, Almost Monday and The Linda Lindas also will be headliners at this year’s event, which will take place Dec. 12 at the Kia Forum in Los Angeles. KROQ, the legendary alternative rock station in Los Angeles that’s owned by Audacy, is bringing the event back to Southern California for its 35th year. The annual event also gives back to the local community, with proceeds benefiting Para Los Niños and Al Wooten Jr. Youth Center. Related Stories Music Young Miko Gets Flirty With L.A. During Her Late Checkout Tour Music Miley Cyrus Returns to the Stage With Emotional and Cathartic Hollywood Bowl Show Founded in 1980 in Skid Row, Los Angeles, Para Los Niños partners with children, youth, and their families through integrated education, wellness, support and advocacy to address individual and systemic barriers and create pathways to success. The Al Wooten Jr. Youth Center in Los Angeles hosts free after-school and low-cost summer programs, through which it revitalizes and empowers communities in crisis by providing a safe, nurturing environment committed to good citizenship and academic excellence. “Almost Acoustic Christmas has always been about the bands and their connection with our listeners,” said Kevin Weatherly, senior vp programming at KROQ. “That’s what makes this show so special, and we’re incredibly grateful to the artists who take the time to be part of it. Celebrating 35 years of this together is pretty amazing. And to be able to give back to two great organizations supporting local youth makes it that much more meaningful.” Tickets go on sale at noon Oct. 30. THR

title: Edward Berger Says Movie Biz “Needed Netflix To Wake Up” But Studios Can Now “Inspire” The Streamer
full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News Dan Lin Is Out As Film Boss At Netflix Read the full story By Jesse Whittock Jesse Whittock International TV Co-Editor @WhittockTweets More Stories By Jesse Ju Ji-hoon & Choo Young-woo Return To ‘The Trauma Code: Heroes On Call’ With Seasons 2 & 3 In Production At Netflix Rafe Spall On Playing An Amnesiac Super Sleuth In ‘The Death Of Sherlock Holmes’: “This Is A Clean Slate” Hudson Williams, Zach Galifianakis & Jay Baruchel Set For ‘The Assembly’ Season 2 At Canada’s CBC View All October 19, 2026 8:48am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Edward Berger Violeta Sofia The movie business “needed Netflix to wake up”, according to Edward Berger , but the Oscar-winning All Quiet on the Western Front director predicted it could be the Hollywood studios inspiring the streaming service in years to come. Related Stories News Netflix Dismisses Dan Lin As Film Boss Before Peter Rice Arrives Executives Netflix Names Peter Rice As Chief Content Officer Speaking today during a fireside chat at the MIA Market in Rome, Berger offered an assessment of how Netflix, which greenlit Oscar winner All Quiet , had impacted Hollywood with its global streaming model. “The movie business needed Netflix to wake up,” he said. “They needed a real disruptor. They had probably become complacent and thought, ‘Okay, let’s do this because it was successful [before]’.” Netflix last week underwent its largest round of layoffs since 2022 – around 1,000 – incidentally the same year World War II pic All Quiet released. With Paramount and Warner Bros. recently becoming one under the Skydance banner and David Ellison promising to make 30 films a year, the wheel could be turning the other way. Watch on Deadline Berger didn’t comment directly on the market, but noted: “Maybe we are now entering a period where the relationship works the other way around, with Netflix being inspired by the movie business. I think the two worlds are additive.” Berger recalled how Sasha Bühler, Netflix’s Director of Film for German-speaking Europe at the time All Quiet was on the market, gave him a simple assessment of how the streamer would handle the film . “She said, ‘If the movie’s great, we’ll support it. If it’s not, we won’t.’ That’s so scary, but I really love that,” he added. Berger called his experience with All Quiet and Netflix “singularly great, with no stress at all.” He praised the streamer for giving “a considerable amount of money for a German film – money we could not have raised in that environment through local or international sales,” coming just as the Covid-19 outbreak was beginning. “Without that support, we might not have been able to make the movie,” he added. The film ultimately won the Best International Film category at the 2023 Oscars. Bühler, who helmed it for Netflix, exited the streamer in August this year, as we revealed at the time. How an Italian actor changed ‘ Conclave ‘ Conclave director Berger charmed a room of Italian delegates today at the MIA Market with a humorous tale from the set of the Oscar-nominated pic, which filmed in Rome. He and his team were searching for a male Italian actor over the age of 65 who spoke English. “The list was very short,” he recalled to laughs from the room. Sergio Castellitto was recommended to play Cardinal Tedesco, and soon given the role. It quickly became clear that Castellitto’s English was limited, but this led to an unexpected change of direction for the movie. Castellitto began changing lines from English into Italian, and with just days to go before filming, the decision was made to add the language. “We had an all-English cast and Sergio was speaking basically only Italian,” he laughed. Ralph Fiennes, who was leading the cast as Cardinal Thomas Lawrence, then decided he would need to quickly learn Italian, so he could respond naturally. “No one was going to go and say, ‘We’re going to stop the film,'” said Berger. It has been a busy few years for Berger, with another bustling period coming up. We were first with the news that Berger had given the World War Z sequel impetus by being attached as director, with Brad Pitt returning to star. The original film, released in 2013, was based on Max Brooks’ bestselling 2006 novel World War Z: An Oral History of the Zombie War . Pitt, Dede Gardner and Jeremy Kleiner are producing the sequel on behalf of Plan B Entertainment. Berger will also executive produce. Dennis Kelly will write the script. Berger is also attached to direct the untitled Lance Armstrong movie package starring Austin Butler as the disgraced cyclist, with Apple winning a heated auction . He will also direct Itamar Moses’ Netflix pic Stradivarius . Berger is headlining this year’s MIA Market in Rome alongside the likes of Jane Tranter. The event begins today and runs through October 23. title: ‘Carrie’ Star Alison Thornton Knows Exactly How You Feel About Her Polarizing Character
full_text: Skip to main content Breaking News Netflix Film Head Dan Lin Out close Alison Thornton Jenna Berman Logo text Alison Thornton is fully embracing the divided online discourse provoked by her polarizing character in Prime Video ‘s Carrie . The Vancouver native actress, who is in the midst of continued press for Mike Flanagan ‘s series adaptation of Stephen King’s classic, which was released on Prime Video on Oct. 7, knows her Chris Hargensen villain role has given viewers moral whiplash. “Some people hate Chris, some people forgive Chris, some people want to give her a hug, and some people cheer when she dies,” Thornton tells The Hollywood Reporter, laughing. Related Stories Beyond the Book Inside Tubi's Plan to Build an R.L. Stine Cinematic Universe TV Amazon Orders Tennis Drama 'Rally' From Julie Plec and Andre Agassi The 27-year-old actress has an array of onscreen credits already, including Girlfriends’ Guide to Divorce , Dare Me and School Spirits . However, her portrayal of the tragic villain in Flanagan’s adaptation of King’s Carrie felt like a stroke of destiny. Thornton revealed that the iconic author was a “huge deal” in her household while growing up. “My mom is the biggest Stephen King fan, and I grew up reading a lot of his books . … I had actually read Carrie twice before even auditioning,” she shares. Despite being familiar with the story of the bullied teen with telekinetic powers, reading the script for Flanagan’s take on the horror caught the actress off guard, realizing how his expanded version added new layers of depth to the ensemble of characters originally introduced in the 1974 novel and its previous film adaptations. Flanagan’s Carrie marks the first time the novel has been reimagined for the small screen with the cast also including Summer H. Howell and Samantha Sloyan. The role of Chris Hargensen has been portrayed by Nancy Allen, Emilie de Ravin and Portia Doubleday in previous screen versions of the book, but in Flanagan’s Carrie , viewers see a more developed Chris, and chronicling how her internal conflicts leads her to a path of tragic disaster. Thornton has been navigating the whirlwind of attention surrounding her role at the heart of the show’s intense discourse. “The response has been incredible. I love seeing people argue about the characters, about who’s morally wrong and who’s morally right. All the conversations around redemption and kindness versus cruelty are exactly what we wanted,” she says. Throughout Flanagan’s eight-episode series, each of the characters are placed at the center of a complex moral debate, continually forced to choose between kindness and cruelty. As their interpersonal dynamics fray, a constant tug-of-war between power and vulnerability not only shapes the characters’ individual choices, but also profoundly impacts their ultimate journeys and tragic fates. Thornton’s Chris journey is one that reflects a tragic spiral and fate. But the series’ choice to humanize the villain without excusing her actions was intentional, Thornton explains. “Reasons are not excuses,” she says. Though she even admits, “If I knew her, I’d want to give her a hug and also yell at her.” In a chat with THR , Thornton reflects on the divisiveness over her character, the parallel journey of Chris and Carrie and responds to those Christine theories. It’s been a little while since the show came out. What have you made of the response, and how are you feeling now that it’s out there for audiences to watch? It’s so wild that the show is finally out, because we shot it over a year ago. The response has been incredible. I love seeing people argue about the characters, about who’s morally wrong and who’s morally right. All the conversations around redemption and kindness versus cruelty are exactly what we wanted. Some people hate Chris, some people forgive Chris, some people want to give her a hug, and some people cheer when she dies. (Laughs.) I love the debate around her. The conversation is really meaningful to me. Take me back to the start. Were you familiar with the Carrie book and the other adaptations? What did you think of the story overall? I was very familiar with Carrie going into this. Stephen King is a huge deal in my household. My mom is the biggest Stephen King fan, and I grew up reading a lot of his books. I’d seen the Brian De Palma movie and the 2013 movie, and I had actually read Carrie twice before even auditioning, so I went in thinking I knew exactly what it was going to be. Then I read Mike [Flanagan]’s scripts, and seeing how much time we had with the characters and how three-dimensional everyone was, I was blown away. I was also a fan of Mike Flanagan, so I was over the moon to be in the Flanniverse and the Stephen King universe. The characters aren’t necessarily what I was expecting from the book, which was such a treat to play. Everyone is so layered. In the show we get to learn Chris’s home dynamic. Her mother is no longer in the picture, and her father is there but not a loving, present figure. Can you talk about the Chris we first meet and how this family dynamic has impacted her? The family dynamic is a huge reason for the choices Chris makes. Working with Michael Trucco and Heather Graham was a dream. One thing I thought was so important is that Chris has truly been shielded from facing any consequences her whole life. Her dad has always covered everything up for her, so I don’t think she understands what adult repercussions look like, and I don’t think she understands how much damage she can actually cause, to other people and to herself. Working on the family dynamic and seeing Michael’s portrayal of John Hargensen, I saw just how ruthless he was. They have a winner mentality, and they view cruelty and being mean as power. There were so many moments in the scripts, and in things we found on the day, where the only time Chris feels affection from her dad is when she’s making fun of Brooklyn or being cruel to someone else. That was so interesting to me: her lack of good role models and her lack of emotional support at home. In the very first scene where we meet Chris and John, Chris doesn’t get breakfast from her dad. She ends up getting a burrito from Sue (Siena Agudong). She really doesn’t have any parental figures at home, which is tragic for her. “She’s such a product of how she was raised, which of course doesn’t justify anything she does, because she does really unforgivable things,“ Thornton says of her villain character. Jenna Berman At school, Chris projects a strong, unfazed persona. She has popularity, power and a following, while Carrie is the complete opposite, someone who can easily become a target. The saying is hurt people hurt people. Do you think Carrie is just a bystander Chris chooses to project her hurt and anger onto, and that it could easily have been someone else? Why Carrie and why not Brooklyn? I love that question, because I really don’t think it has anything to do with Carrie herself. As you said, it’s just bad timing for Carrie. I love that Carrie and Brooklyn look kind of similar, and that Brooklyn is off limits. I think a lot of Chris’s reason for targeting Carrie is how vulnerable she is and also the threat of losing Sue. Carrie enters the picture, and Sue gravitates toward her and shows her all this warmth. I think Chris is really envious of that, especially since she’s losing her support system at home, and Sue has been the only parent and healthy role model Chris has ever had. When that gets threatened, Chris thinks, “I need to push this girl as far away from our friend group as possible and hopefully get Sue back.” There’s also something interesting in Summer’s beautiful portrayal of Carrie and how optimistic she is. She’s so wholesome and genuinely kind, and people start gravitating toward her. Carrie gets more and more popular throughout the show, and I think that’s really threatening to Chris because of how she was raised. She’s been taught that you get power from making people afraid of you and being cruel. Chris has such a sinister view of the world, so seeing this girl come in and truly embody kindness, and that being enough to give her power, is so threatening to Chris’ identity. She can’t handle it. So there are a lot of reasons Chris is unaware of for why she chooses to bully Carrie, but none of them have to do with Carrie herself. Despite being different, Carrie and Chris have more in common than they may think. Both of their parents project their own faults onto their kids, yet Carrie and Chris turn out differently. Carrie wants to escape and be free from her mom, whereas Chris internalizes that cruelty and uses it against others. Do you think Chris could ever see that similarity, that they’re two sides of the same coin? I don’t think Chris has the perspective to see that. She’s so caught up in her own pain and her own world. But I love the parallel between them. One thing I thought was so cool in the scripts is that, as you said, they both lose their emotional support at home in the first episode. They both discover power early on: for Carrie it’s telekinesis, and for Chris it’s social media and bullying. They’re both then influenced by outside forces to do the wrong thing: for Carrie it’s Emaline (Thalia Dudek), and for Chris it’s Billy (Arthur Conti). They’re on a parallel track the whole time. I think one of the most interesting conversations around the show is: once you discover you have that power, whatever it may be, do you use it for good or for bad? I don’t think Chris is old enough or has the maturity to see the tragedy that they could actually have been friends, that they’re quite similar and could have helped each other out. That’s such a shame. The characters all have a choice between kindness and cruelty, yet they all seem to take the more destructive path. Chris takes the cruel path, but it doesn’t always seem solid. There are moments, like with Billy holding the rock over the freeway or wanting to hit Carrie with his car, where she shows hesitance and that there’s still a moral compass there. What did you make of her internal conflict? I think there are many moments in the show where Chris hesitates. One of my favorites is the trench sequence at the construction site. I really don’t think Chris knows how far she’s going to take it. She’s discovering this power as she goes, and she’s being influenced by Billy, who at that point is the only person validating her and giving her any kind of attention. He likes it when she’s cruel, so she plays that up around him, especially once Sue has exited Chris’ life. Chris really needs someone to say, “Hey, you’re OK, you’re enough. All of these dark thoughts, acting on them is the wrong choice.” Billy (portrayed by Arthur Conti) “is the only person validating her and giving her any kind of attention,“ Thornton says of their dynamic. Prime Video I also love how many moments there are where I think Chris is about to apologize. I think she’s about to apologize in the principal’s office. I think she wants so badly to apologize when she’s alone with Carrie in the bathroom. The internal conflict she’s facing is that she wants everything to go away and go back to normal, but she’s also hearing her dad’s voice in her head, the idea that the Hargensens don’t lose, and that if she apologizes, she’s admitting defeat. Combine that with her never actually being held responsible for any of her actions, and it’s a perfect storm. She’s so stubborn that she can’t make things right, which is also very sad to me. There’s something really scary about being at that age, where you don’t really understand the consequences yet, or how much damage you can do through cruelty. She’s facing all of that at the same time, which is unfortunate for her. It does not end well. You mentioned how she wants to go back to normal, but there’s a new normal that she’s unwilling to accept. She has one identity crisis, which will probably be one of many she’d have in life, but it’s so tragic to her that she thinks, “Everything’s over. I can’t handle it.” I think she really needed the promise of going to Duke and getting out of Chamberlain, getting away from her mom and her dad. She needed that so much, especially with Sue. When that falls apart, she’s just like, “Well, I don’t know what to do now. It’s done.” “I saw just how ruthless he was. They have a winner mentality, and they view cruelty and being mean as power,“ Thornton says of Chris‘ father (portrayed by Michael Trucco). Prime Video You brought up the bathroom scene with Carrie. In that moment, Carrie genuinely wants to understand and seems to give Chris the chance to explain so they can move on. It could have been the moment everything changed for the better. Can you talk more about that scene? I love that scene so much. Episode six was the last episode we shot, so we’d been building toward it the whole time. Summer and I kept calling it the real mediation, because the parents hijack the actual mediation. The scene felt so complicated and layered to me. Carrie’s question, “Why me?” is such a fair question, and no one has really asked Chris that. It’s the only scene where Chris and Carrie are alone together, and I think it catches Chris off guard. I don’t think she’s thought about it: why, genuinely, did you do this? At that point she’s dug herself into such a deep hole that I don’t think she can process anything clearly. Carrie does get through to her for a second. Chris is actually reflecting for the first time and almost apologizes, and then at the last minute she pulls back. I remember reading it and wanting to shake her and say, “Come on, you’re so close! You could have fixed everything.” It’s my favorite scene in the show, I think, because it’s when Chris doubles down. After that, it’s the point of no return for her. There’s a scene where it alternates between Chris and Carrie in the car. Carrie is happy and free, allowing herself to be a normal teenager for the first time, lifting the car without even knowing it. In contrast, we see Chris completely breaking down, hiding it from Sue while Sue drives. If she could just show that part of herself, I’d imagine people would be there for her more than she thinks. I totally agree. Chris has unfortunately been taught that vulnerability is weakness. If she could open up to the people around her and lean on Sue. … I think she could benefit from some therapy and just talking about her feelings. She’s such a product of how she was raised, which of course doesn’t justify anything she does, because she does really unforgivable things. That scene is so interesting to me, too, because from Chris’ perspective, that was supposed to be her night, her at her most powerful, running this party. It wasn’t supposed to end with Carrie on top. Chris doesn’t really witness that, but once again it’s the parallel between them. They’re on very similar tracks. They’re two sides of the same coin, essentially. “Working with Michael Trucco and Heather Graham was a dream.“ (Pictured from left: Trucco, Thornton and Heather Graham.) Prime Video With all the characters in the show, there’s an exploration of losing control, taking control and relinquishing control, and Chris experiences all of those. What was Chris’ relationship with control like to you, and how did it shape the path she’s on? She’s seemingly losing control and trying to take it back, but in the wrong way. Chris has always been someone who has had control and power, just because of her family circumstances, and she loses it really quickly in the first episode. I think that’s a big reason she makes the “Carrie Red” account. It’s the only power she has. Bullying Carrie is a new kind of power she finds, essentially the only control in her life. The more followers she gets and the more people send posts to “Carrie Red,” the more she realizes she’s having a pretty large impact, and that feels good, especially since she doesn’t have power in any other part of her life at that moment. As you said, she’s grasping for these morsels of power and control, and she finds them in really destructive places. Do you think her friendship with Sue would have been repairable? We see the moment on the “Carrie Red” social media account where Chris reveals Sue‘s big secret yet we also see Chris learn Sue is the one to betrayed her by recording her admission of being behind the social media account. I would hope so, but I feel like the scars would have been so deep that it would have taken so much work. I think they could use years apart. They have a really co-dependent, really toxic friendship. I do think Chris addresses Sue’s betrayal by posting the photo of Sue’s pregnancy test. It’s a little bit of revenge and a cry for help at the same time. But the damage is so deep in that friendship that I think they should probably separate for a while and see who they are without each other. Chris needed support and love from other people, and she was very dependent on Sue for that. She needed other healthy friendships and role models in her life, too. “They have a really co-dependent, really toxic friendship,“ Thornton says of Chris and Sue (portrayed by Siena Agudong). Prime Video The final scene between Chris and Carrie where Chris is about to die, she attempts to apologize to Carrie. Do you think she was genuinely saying sorry in that moment, or was it an act of desperation to save herself? I think Chris is genuinely sorry. I think of the conversation she has with Billy right before the car flips, when she looks at him and says, “What did we do?” She’s facing so much guilt and remorse, and she’s being forced to see the impact of her actions. In those final moments, she knows what’s going to happen. She knows there’s nothing she can do, and there’s no point in fighting. She just wants to make things as right as possible before she dies. So I think it’s genuine remorse. The show ends on a cliffhanger, and there’s been a lot of online discussion and conspiracy theories about the story’s connections and where it could lead. One is that Chris’ soul possesses Billy’s car at her death and turns it into Stephen King’s famous killer car, Christine. Have you heard that? Do you have thoughts? I’ve heard that one, and I really like it. It’s so exciting. The evil car, of course. I trust Mike Flanagan. Whatever he thinks for season two is in his hands. But I do love the conspiracy theories. I love seeing people say, “They’re wearing the same necklace! What does that mean?” People keep sending me screenshots of conspiracy theories asking, “What is this?” And I’m like, “I don’t know. I didn’t notice that either.” (Laughs.) I do think the Christine connection makes the most sense. I could play a car for a few hours in hair and makeup, easy! I’m so here for it! This show’s version of Chris is one where we can humanize her and understand how she became this deeply broken person, but we can also still not excuse a single thing she does. After playing her, do you feel protective of her? What do you make of playing a character that people can be conflicted over? She’s polarizing.I have very complicated feelings. What I was really holding on to is that reasons are not excuses. We see her reasoning, and I understand her decision-making, and she’s also making the wrong choices. When I was playing her, the only way to play her was to have so much empathy for her. If I knew her, I’d want to give her a hug and also yell at her. I feel so bad for her. I really think her death is a tragedy, and it’s a tragedy also because she’ll never be able to make things right. My interpretation is that I would have loved to see her go to juvie, get some therapy, do community service and then actually get on a better path. I was never cheering for her to die. There are moments in the show where I’m like, “What are you doing? Please stop. This is cruel.” But, again, reasons are not excuses. And I love that she’s polarizing. It’s so fun. I imagine things are still very Carrie -focused right now, but what are you working on, and what roles and stories are you hoping to tell? I imagine this feels like a big chapter in your career, and hopefully one of many. I can’t say too much. I do have a movie coming out soon called And Love Knocked , but there are a few things on the horizon that I can’t share yet. Carrie was a dream project with dream collaborators: the cast, Mike Flanagan, Stephen King. It was such a dream role and such a pivotal chapter in my life, and it was a masterclass to work with everyone. Right now I’m just in Carrie world and reveling in that. We shall see! Mike Flanagan is known for having his staple ensembles and teaming with the same actors in different projects. Is there another story he could take on that you’d love to be part of? I would love to work with him on anything! He’s such an incredible director and a great guy, and I’d love to keep working with him. The cast of actors he works with are all so phenomenal. I keep saying I would love a Pet Sematary remake, because it’s my favorite Stephen King book, so I’m putting it out there! About those Christine rumors: “I could play a car for a few hours in hair and makeup, easy! I’m so here for it!“ Jenna Berman THR

title: Rosie O’Donnell and Kristin Chenoweth Join ‘Dance Moms’ Parody Musical Reading (EXCLUSIVE)
full_text: Oct 19, 2026 8:45am PT Rosie O’Donnell and Kristin Chenoweth Join ‘Dance Moms’ Parody Musical Reading (EXCLUSIVE) By Marc Malkin Plus Icon Marc Malkin Senior Editor, Culture and Events marcmalkin Latest Rosie O’Donnell and Kristin Chenoweth Join ‘Dance Moms’ Parody Musical Reading (EXCLUSIVE) 36 minutes ago Inde Navarrette on Meeting Pamela Anderson, Hosting ‘SNL’ and X-Men Stunt Training 16 hours ago KJ Apa on Becoming Jimmy Stewart, Speculation That He Is the Singer Mr. Fantasy and Opening Up About His Addictions and Recovery: ‘This Is A Huge Part of Who I Am’ 2 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Doreen Kilfeather Rosie O’Donnell and Kristin Chenoweth have joined the cast for a reading of “The Pyramid: An Unauthorized ‘Dance Moms’ Musical.” O’Donnell is said to be playing embattled instructor and series star Abby Lee Miller while Tony winner Chenoweth will take on the role of Cathy Nesbitt-Stein, a fellow instructor who quit the reality show after the first season. The reading takes place Monday afternoon in New York City. O’Donnell teased the reading in a recent TikTok video, saying that she and Chenoweth were signed on for a reading of a new musical without naming the show. Popular on Variety Related Stories Record and Song of the Year Grammy Predictions: With Ella Langley, Taylor Swift, the Two Olivias and Other Frontrunners in the Race, Expect a Nail-Biter Taylor Swift to Perform at Academy Museum Gala O’Donnell recently wrapped up a limited run as the narrator in the Broadway revival of “The Rocky Horror Picture Show.” Originally conceived by James Stryska and Isabel Grace, “The Pyramid” began as a viral social media concept that quickly amassed more than 5.6 million views. Developed alongside cowriters Erica Molfetto and Molly Russo, the original musical offers an irreverent take on competitive dance, overzealous stage mothers and the larger-than-life personalities that made “ Dance Moms ” a cultural phenomenon. “Dance Moms” premiered in 2011 on Lifetime and ran for eight seasons before ending in 2019. Miller became a controversial figure who was often criticized for her harsh teaching lessons and her treatment of the students and their mothers. She served time in prison after being charged with multiple financial crimes. O’Donnell and Chenoweth’s involvement follows the previously announced addition of Tye Blue, the Tony-nominated co-creator of the Broadway hit “Titaníque,” who joined the production as creative producer earlier this year. Logan Clark and Tye Blue. The production is led by television producer and casting director Logan Clark, whose credits include “Beast Games,” “The Masked Singer,” “The Floor,” “American Idol” and “America’s Got Talent.” Clark began his career working on the original “Dance Moms” series. Clark’s company, The Casting Collective, is overseeing the nationwide casting initiative for the musical. title: Netflix Film Head Dan Lin Out
full_text: × Skip to main content Breaking News Netflix Film Head Dan Lin Out close By Mia Galuppo Plus Icon Mia Galuppo Senior Entertainment Reporter miagaluppo Follow Sign Up View All October 19, 2026 8:38am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Dan Lin Jon Kopaloff/Getty Images for American Cinematheque Dan Lin is out as Netflix ‘s film chief, sources tell The Hollywood Reporter . The news comes as the streamer cuts from its uppermost ranks and implements layoffs that will affect roughly 1,000 people, the company’s biggest cut since 2022. Prior to Lin, chief content officer Bela Bajaria was exited, along with VP of film Doug Belgrad and a series of high-ranking television executives. It is unclear who will assume Lin’s role, but the understanding is that Peter Rice, who took over the chief content officer post, will be in charge of finding new leadership. Netflix did not immediately reply for comment. Lin joined Netflix in 2024, taking over from then film chief Scott Stuber. Under Stuber, Netflix became known as the place where name filmmakers could land big budgets and paydays as the traditional studios implemented more cost-conscious spending practices. During this time, the streamer consistently ended up with best picture nominations, but top awards have notoriously evaded Netflix films. Lin, who was hired by Bajaria, was brought in to curb spending while (ideally) increasing the quality of the entire film slate, not just the titles from big-name directors. Under Lin, the streamer‘s movies division was reorganized by genre , with deputies like Kira Goldberg and Niija Kuykendall handling films that fell under categories like sci-fi, rom-com and family film. Netflix began offering more mid-size films that have been ignored by theatrical players, including big book adaptations like Remarkably Bright Creatures and People We Meet on Vacation , as well as mid-budget action films like Apex and The RIP. (This is not to say that Netflix’s Lin tenure was without big swings — see: Greta Gerwig‘s Narnia movie due out next year or David Fincher’s The Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth — but the offerings no doubt slowed.) Lin came from his production company Rideback, which minted the $1 billion grossing Aladdin and was involved in the hit It movies as well as The Lego Movies . He departed the company when he joined Netflix, leaving partners at the helm who found another $1 billion hit with last summer’s live-action Lilo & Stitch . Presumably, he could return to Rideback now that his Netflix tenure is up. As of late, the streamer hasn’t been able to capture audience interest, at least at the rate co-CEO Ted Sarandos would like, with viewership and subscriber growth stagnant. Under Rice‘s leadership, Netflix will focus on “creating big, buzzy hits,“ as Sarandos wrote in his memo to staff. THR

Insiders at the streamer have denied that Dan Lin and even Bela Bajaria were on the chopping block, but here we are. At Saturday night’s Academy Museum Gala cocktails, we caught up with Netflix co-CEO Ted Sarandos and asked if more cuts were coming. In what seemed like a polite dodge, he just winked and stepped away. Interpret that as you may. Lin’s firing comes in the wake of Netflix making 1,000 pink-slips given their recent slow growth, and minimal overall viewership spike. Wall Street is bracing for what is expected to be a downer quarter from the OTT service. At the time of this post, Netflix shares were trading at $69.76, -1% at the time of this report. It was seen that Belgrad was an extra layer at the top of Netflix’s film brass that could easily be let go, dollar wise. Lin was expected to be safe until Bajaria’s replacement arrived on Oct. 26, Peter Rice. It was at that point in time that the exec was going to assess the situation. Watch on Deadline All of this boils down to: Netflix, what is it you exactly want? All of streaming has turned into basic cable as we get farther away from Covid. They looked to Lin in April 2024 post Scott Stuber in order to ratchet down the quantity of features and at a lower cost. Lin did exactly what they asked, steering away from overpriced $200M-plus, non downstream features like Red Notice, The Irishman and The Electric State . However, he had a no-nonsense approach to filmmakers. He had no problem reportedly pushing back on prestige content creators like Greta Gerwig and Ben Affleck. During the Lin regime, one source told us that relationships with filmmakers were fraying. Recently, The Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth filmmaker David Fincher opted not to renew his longtime exclusive contract with the streamer. During Lin’s run Netflix saw their most viewed movie of all-time, Sony’s Kpop Demon Hunters (325.1M global views). However, that was greenlit under the previous Stuber administration. Lin and Belgrad’s bragging rights include War Machine ($80M production cost, 147M views), animated movie Swapped (144.9M views, which broke into the streamer’s top 10 of all-time), The Rip ($100M production cost, 136M views), Happy Gilmore 2 (135.1M), Apex (129M), Thrash (100M views) and People We Meet on Vacation ($14M production cost, 77.1M). Still there wasn’t a consistent reseeding of the Top 10 Most Popular list like there was during the Stuber era. The Mike and Pam Of It All After being passed over by Skydance for top jobs at the new Paramount Warner Bros. post-merger, we hear that former WB Motion Picture Bosses Michael De Luca and Pamela Abdy are in the home stretch this week of finalizing the payout of their WB contracts by David Ellison. Until they’re closed, they can’t entertain any job offers. Those close to De Luca tell us he’d have no problems reporting into Rice if offered the job, however, Netflix would need to make a fire-breathing commitment to theatrical. The notion of a 45-day theatrical window to streaming isn’t a prospect that De Luca (and Abdy) could make to the filmmakers they’ve worked with, i.e. Ryan Coogler, Paul Thomas Anderson, Ridley Scott. The notion that the duo are bound to raise capital for their own feature operation seems like the more practical future for them. All this smoke over De Luca and Abdy heading to Netflix came about due to a friendly lunch with Sarandos. This has morphed into gossip that Sarandos was full-on courting the duo. If Sarandos and Rice bring the filmmaker-friendly duo in, the question is whether they’ll put any guardrails on them. When it came to De Luca and Abdy justifying the lofty costs for Anderson’s One Battle After Another, Coogler’s Sinners, Tom Cruise’s Digger and so on, David Zaslav didn’t blink an eye. Will Sarandos allow them the same greenlight independence he granted Stuber? Or will he expect them to count coins like Lin? Riddle us that, Mr. Sarandos. “Netflix isn’t a place where they talk about film,” says one creator who has worked with them, “They’re all about the process, the algorithm and breaking the code, which still makes Lin a good workhorse for them as he’s also about process.” There’s a rumor out there, and that is despite the notion that De Luca and Abdy are always joined at the hip, historically they haven’t been. Some believe there’s a world that Abdy could entertain an offer sans De Luca from Netflix once her WB contract is paid out. “Sure, there is a world where that could happen,” says one source with knowledge of the situation. Still, there’s no solid definite word out there as to who might fill Lin’s vacancy. No interview process going on as of yet. A rival studio boss complimented over the weekend, “I think you’ll be surprised as to who Peter Rice selects.” But still, no matter how the greenlight process is improved at Netflix, there’s a new sign of the times for the streamer. “If you want to know where the young crowd is looking, Meta just introduced Muse. People are heading back to cinemas, and streaming has become basic cable,” said one Netflix vet, “They can change shuffle as many executives as they want, and it still won’t make a difference.” Sources in the know have confirmed Lin’s firing to us. title: Lance Armstrong On Schwinn Bicycles Documentary ‘No Hands’: “It’s An Incredible American Story”
full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News Dan Lin Is Out As Film Boss At Netflix Read the full story By Stewart Clarke Stewart Clarke More Stories By Stewart ‘Tall Tales & Murder’ Scores New International Deals As Season 2 Takes Shape Cineverse Boards Genre-Bending Holiday Film ‘Ralph’s Perfekt Christmas’ From ‘Grey’s Anatomy’ To Scottish Indie Boss: Kevin McKidd On Ferryman Films & His New Show ‘The Only Suspect’ View All October 19, 2026 8:37am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Lance Armstrong narrates 'No Hands: The Wild Ride of the Schwinn Bicycle Company' Schwinn Doc LLC EXCLUSIVE: No Hands : The Wild Ride of the Schwinn Bicycle Company documents the extraordinary tale of the titular bike brand with Lance Armstrong serving as both an interview subject and narrator. Armstrong tells Deadline about this rags-to-riches-to-bankruptcy tale and how things could have been different for the iconic brand if he had been on board a Schwinn as he raced the Tour de France , in turn creating a boom in the U.S. market for road bicycles. “It doesn’t have the greatest ending for the family, but it’s an incredible American story,” he says of the feature documentary. “It’s the story of an immigrant. It’s the story of starting from scratch. It’s also the story – and I love thinking about this – of the importance of the bicycle on American culture, and I think sometimes that’s lost on people.” Related Stories News Tour De France: Tadej Pogacar Dominates Race For Record-Tying Fifth Win News Paramount's 5 Pacts With WBD's TNT Sports For Tour De France Highlights Unfeatured Films founder Daniel Clarke directs the film, which comes from the people behind The Lego Brickumentary , narrated by Jason Bateman, and Loopers: The Caddie’s Long Walk , which was narrated by Bill Murray. Watch on Deadline “There are a few brands in the history of whatever that have really owned the category, or, said another way, have named the category,” Armstrong says of Schwinn. And the feature doc duly shows how ingrained in U.S. culture Schwinn became as it got to a point of making over a million bikes a year. “Schwinn equals bike, bike equals Schwinn,” Armstrong said of its glory years. He got involved in No Hands: The Wild Ride of the Schwinn Bicycle Company via Jim Packer , the Lionsgate exec who is an EP on the documentary, which uses AI to bring historical pictures and sequences to life. Deadline has a first look at the trailer (see below) as the film embarks on a festival run. No Hands recounts how Ignaz Schwinn traveled from Germany to the U.S. and, in 1895, he and Adolph Arnold launched the iconic bike brand, setting a manufacturing base in Chicago. Different generations will get misty-eyed over various models Schwinn produced, from the humble safety bike to the Sting-Ray, which took its design cues from American muscle cars, to sleek race bikes such as the Paramount. Armstrong, a veteran of the world’s biggest bike races, has his own memories: “I did the [1989] Junior World Champs on a Paramount, and to this day, for whatever reason, I still think that’s the best riding bike that I’ve ever ridden.” The film shows how Schwinn was cutting edge in many ways. The brand leaned into what would now be called influencer marketing, with the likes of Roy Rogers, Frank Sinatra and Joan Crawford seen aboard their bikes. It pioneered having its own stores – nowadays the A-list bike brands have their own concept stores – and it had groundbreaking designs and detailing. Having gotten generations of people onto two wheels, it had huge influence on BMX, mountain biking and cutting-edge design, but did not capitalize on these trends as they changed the face of cycling. Armstrong’s succinct take captures it: “They were innovative until they weren’t.” He rode a Trek bicycle in multiple editions of the Tour de France and cycling’s other blue ribband events. As U.S. audiences saw their man in the Yellow Jersey, sales at the likes of Trek and Specialized exploded. But Schwinn had been left in their dust, filing for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in 1992. The Schwinn brand continued under new ownership after the bankruptcy and the No Hands filmmakers said they have no relationship with the current Schwinn Bicycle Company. “There’s a world where, somehow, they had agreed to offshore production, or got into the carbon game, and if they had done that in those early years…if that was a Schwinn instead of a Trek [I was riding], we would 100% be having a very different conversation,” Armstrong says. Sadly for Schwinn, that was not the case, but the rise and fall story takes in how a family business became a cultural icon. No Hands: The Wild Ride of the Schwinn Bicycle Company opens with scenes from film and TV that reference Schwinn, underlining how it became shorthand for cycling. Director Clarke says his film “is the love letter to Schwinn that generations of kids deserve.” He adds: “The documentary feature explores Schwinn’s storied history, from the iconic Sting-Ray to its widespread influence in the worlds of BMX and mountain biking. “Through the accounts of fans, collectors, cycling pioneers and the Schwinn family themselves, No Hands tells the story of a brand that changed cycling forever and survived through the struggles of American manufacturing, family drama, fads and business forces that ultimately led to its bankruptcy.” Armstrong was keen to get involved. “I watch probably an unhealthy amount of documentaries, so there’s just my general interest in the category, and then obviously I had a touchpoint here, I have a lot of history with this brand.” Having been the subject of numerous docs, this was new for Armstrong in that here, he is narrating and being interviewed, and the doc isn’t focused on him. “I thought it was a fun thing to try. You hope the audience appreciates it. I think the film is great. I enjoyed the hell out of being a little bit involved in the process, obviously sitting for the interview, but then just getting in the studio and recording the narration.” While No Hands is a family story, a business story, a sports story and a story about moments in history, ultimately, it taps into the simple and timeless joy of riding bicycles, with which Schwinn is synonymous. The simple premise is: you never forget your first bike. In the film, Armstrong talks about the excitement and freedom that a first bike can bring. Decades later, the fire lit by his first steed, a brown Schwinn Mag Scrambler, still burns bright. “It’s not lost on anybody, my history with the bicycle, with the sport, with all of the races, with the Tour, all of the things associated with it,” he says. “Still to this day, at 55 years old, if I can wake up and go for a bike ride … and it borders on sounding a little corny, but when I talk about how that makes me feel, how that is still an escape for me, in many ways, it is like church.” No Hands comes from Tiburon Productions and Gem Pictures in association with Brookwell McNamara Entertainment and KSQD Media, and is produced by Human Design. Packer is an EP alongside Chris Brown, David Brookwell, Carl Cramer, Khristian A. Howell and George K. Howell. title: CNN Shocker: Christiane Amanpour to Exit News Channel Next Year
full_text: × Skip to main content Breaking News Netflix Film Head Dan Lin Out close By Alex Weprin Plus Icon Alex Weprin Senior Editor alexweprin Follow Sign Up View All October 19, 2026 8:26am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Christiane Amanpour Photo by Sean Gallup/Getty Images CNN is losing one of its highest-profile anchors and correspondents next year. Christiane Amanpour will scale back her work at CNN over the next few months, and leave the channel entirely next June. CNN CEO Mark Thompson shared the news in a note to staff Monday morning. “Christiane has thought carefully about this decision, and she and I have been discussing it for some months,” he wrote. “Like so many CNNers who will hear the news today, I’m very sorry to see her go, but I’ve come to accept that this is the right time for her, both personally and professionally.” Amanpour has been with CNN for 43 years, becoming perhaps its most famous foreign correspondent, and a staple of its lineup. Why Amanpour is leaving is not clear, but the announcement comes just weeks after Skydance completed its acquisition of Warner bros. Discovery, bringing CNN into its fold. Thompson will continue to lead CNN for the time being, though longer-term anything could happen. “After many months of thought and a few sleepless nights, I have decided to separate from CNN, my partner of 43 fantastic years!” she said in a statement. “I will end my daily shows across CNN and PBS at the end of this year, while continuing to maintain a weekly show on CNN through May and working on a smooth transition through June. Amanpour had publicly expressed concern with the takeover, saying at an event in May that “Clearly I’m concerned, and I’m not sure how much I’m allowed to say about a corporate thing that’s under way, but I am obviously, as a person, as a journalist with a record, concerned, and I’m concerned based on what’s happened to the other things that [Ellison has] taken over already, like CBS News.” For now, she will gradually pull back on her CNN International show this year bfore it ends next May. She will continue to host her podcast The Ex Filed, which she co-hosts with her ex-husband and former U.S. diplomat and Assistant Secretary of State Jamie Rubin. The podcast is not produced by CNN. “I want to thank all the amazingly talented people I’ve worked with throughout this incredible journey. Especially my beloved show teams and field crews,” she continued. “From my very first big exciting assignment covering the First Gulf War, to the horrors of the Bosnian War, Rwanda, Afghanistan, Ukrain and Iran and all the points in between, it’s the teams and the camaraderie that counted so much, as we together battled to seek the facts, the evidence and the humanity, so that CNN could always broadcast the truth about the world and to the world, without fear nor favor.” You can read Thompson’s note to staff below. Dear all, I’m writing today with news about a CNN icon – and our dear friend and colleague – Christiane Amanpour. After more than 43 years at CNN, Christiane has decided that the time is right to begin a new chapter. Early in 2027, she will scale back her CNN International show, Amanpour, to once a week. The program will conclude in May, and she will leave CNN at the end of June. Christiane has thought carefully about this decision, and she and I have been discussing it for some months. Like so many CNNers who will hear the news today, I’m very sorry to see her go, but I’ve come to accept that this is the right time for her, both personally and professionally. Christiane has been a household name around the world for decades. Yet she began more than 40 years ago not as one of the biggest stars in CNN’s history, but as a news desk assistant in our Atlanta newsroom. Famously, one of her bosses told her back then that she didn’t have what it took to become a foreign correspondent – or to hold any on-air role at all. Boy, did she prove him wrong! It would be impossible to list all of her reporting triumphs, exclusive interviews, awards and broadcasting firsts, or the many other accomplishments that have made her one of the most trusted and beloved journalists anywhere. We will make sure to share and celebrate them all before she departs next year. In the meantime, on behalf of the entire CNN leadership team, I want to thank Christiane for 43 extraordinary years of remarkable journalism, loyalty and friendship. Mark THR

full_text: Oct 19, 2026 8:16am PT Christiane Amanpour to Exit CNN in June After 43 Years By Brian Steinberg Plus Icon Brian Steinberg Senior TV Editor bristei Latest Christiane Amanpour to Exit CNN in June After 43 Years 46 minutes ago CBS News Correspondent Jan Crawford Apologizes for Post on Abdul El-Sayed That Sparked Social-Media Ire 22 hours ago Odell Beckham Jr. Taps Range Sports for Off-Field Opportunities 4 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source David Vintiner for Variety Christiane Amanpour , who parlayed a job as a news assistant on CNN ‘s foreign desk into a years-long globe-trotting assignment for the news giant, plans to step away from the media company in June. “After many months of thought and a few sleepless nights, I have decided to separate from CNN, my partner of 43 fantastic years!” Amanpour said in a statement Monday. She added that she “looks forward to interesting new projects down the line, and will always be rooting for CNN and maintaining its history of independent journalism. Remember: always be truthful, not neutral.” Related Stories Taylor Swift's 'Patient Zero' Holds Steady at No. 1 for Second Week on Singles Chart Graham Norton Shoots Down ‘Conspiracy Theory’ That Taylor Swift’s ‘Opalite’ Video Was Shot Before She Came on His Show Amanpour’s exit is announced just as CNN comes under the control of a new owner, Skydance , which is grappling with billions of dollars in debt and perceptions that it may want to skew its news operations toward a particular view on politics and other issues. Popular on Variety Amanpour, 68 years old, has hosted both an evening program for CNN’s international channel since 2009 and a show for PBS, “Amanpour & Company,” since 2017. She left CNN briefly for an ill-fated run at ABC News, where she was named moderator of the Sunday program, “The Week,” in 2010. Low ratings undermined her efforts there, and she returned to CNN in 2012. “Christiane has thought carefully about this decision, and she and I have been discussing it for some months,” said Mark Thompson, CEO of CNN, in a statement. “Like so many CNNers who will hear the news today, I’m very sorry to see her go, but I’ve come to accept that this is the right time for her, both personally and professionally.” CNN employs many journalists, correspondents and anchors, but few of them are as tied to the news outlet’s overall brand as Amanpour. Perhaps only Wolf Blitzer and Anderson Cooper enjoy similar status among present staffers. After securing a role in eastern Europe in 1986, she made a reputation for herself by covering conflicts in Bosnia, Iraq and Afghanistan. From 1992 to 2010, she worked as CNN’s chief international correspondent. “I will end my daily shows across CNN and PBS at the end of this year, while continuing to maintain a weekly show on CNN through May and working on a smooth transition through June,” Amanpour said in her note Monday. She indicated that she expects to continue working on an independent podcast, “Ex-Files,” which she leads along with her ex-husband, Jamie Rubin, former official at the U.S. State Department. Strong has been named the new in-venue show announcer for the Westminster Kennel Club Dog Show , The Hollywood Reporter has learned, which returns to New York City in early 2027 with its 151st installment. Strong, who has called the FIFA World Cup and Major League Soccer (MLS), succeeds Michael J. LaFave as the “Voice of Westminster.” LaFave put 25 years into the role. As announced in May, the Westminster dog show will stream on Netflix . The Westminster Kennel Club Dog Show is the second-longest continuously held sporting event, behind only the Kentucky Derby. We know he will bring his signature flair, expert commentary and genuine love of dogs to every moment leading up to Best in Show.” “I am humbled and honored to step into this prestigious role for The Westminster Kennel Club,” added Strong. “I look forward to honoring the legacy of Westminster and celebrating the future of this beloved sporting event while lending my passion for dogs and live sports experience to the world’s top canine competitors.” “Bark! The daytime breed competitions at the Jacob K. Javits Convention Center will stream live on The Westminster Kennel Club’s website and YouTube channel.
