title: ‘Smallville’ at 25: Tom Welling and Michael Rosenbaum on Clark Kent and Lex Luthor’s Origin Story, the Journey to Superman and That Final Moment
full_text: Dan Doperalski for Variety A little more than 25 years ago, on Oct. 16, 2021, “ Smallville ” premiered on The WB. Created by Alfred Gough and Miles Millar, and based on the DC Comics character, the show set out to do something that’s now common practice but was then novel: tell the origin story of an iconic character, enriching the character’s mythology along the way. On the show, an immediate hit for the network, Tom Welling and Michael Rosenbaum played, respectively, a high-school-aged Clark Kent and his eventual nemesis Lex Luthor in the fictional town of Smallville, Kansas. One of the inventions of “Smallville” is that Clark (who yearns to be ordinary) and Lex (who lives under the thumb of his controlling zillionaire father) are, for a time, best friends, before the inevitable happens, as Lex succumbs to his darker instincts. “I felt like I had the liberty to just do what I wanted to do, and be real, and grounded,” Rosenbaum said in a recent interview. “I mean, seeing Lex and Clark as friends — and then obviously we know what happens with the relationship, but I thought it was really fascinating. It had never been done.” As opposed to their characters, Welling and Rosenbaum remain close: They host a “Smallville” rewatch podcast called “TalkVille,” and the night before they came to the Variety office, Welling, who doesn’t live in Los Angeles, had stayed at Rosenbaum’s house. They’ve been celebrating the show’s 25th anniversary, and in their most extensive conversation together about the show’s legacy, they filmed a “How Well Do They Know Each Other?” video, answering questions about one another and about “Smallville.” During the game, they flopped on things like the show’s premiere date (somehow, Welling’s first answer was Oct. 14 , 1992 , before he switched it to that same date in 2002) and its ratings, which broke records for The WB. The correct answer was that 8.4 million total viewers tuned in live, but Rosenbaum wrote “12 million, Beeyotch,” and Welling wrote “1 trillion,” then trying to explain by saying, “Well, I mean, worldwide.” Rosenbaum harangued him. “You know how much a trillion is? A trillion is like, a lot of billions,” he said. “Dude, if we had those ratings, we’d still be on the air. Good lord.” As they reminisced, they talked about the guest stars who’d appeared on “Smallville” over its 10 seasons, some already well known, others new to the business. One of them, in a loving tribute to Superman ’s long history, was Christopher Reeve, who appeared twice on the show as billionaire scientist Dr. Virgil Swann, Clark’s mentor. Well before superhero movies became ubiquitous, Reeve had his breakthrough role as Clark Kent in the 1978 “Superman” film, a blockbuster, and played him three more times in its sequels. In 1995, however, Reeve, a competitive equestrian, had a devastating accident, breaking his spine while riding, and becoming paralyzed for the rest of his life. (He died in 2004.) Related Stories Taylor Swift's 'Patient Zero' Bumps 'Choosin' Texas' Out of No. 1 on Hot 100; 'Encore' Tracks Fill Four Out of Five Top Slots Taylor Swift to Perform at Academy Museum Gala Dan Doperalski for Variety Welling said he’d filmed the scenes with Reeve in New York, and they bonded. “We talked a lot about what it meant to play the character,” he said. “He said he was really happy that they chose me to play the role, which I thought was cool.” Popular on Variety The “Smallville” production wanted to make things easy for Reeve, Welling said, with him filming his part of the scene and then leaving. “But he wanted to stay for my coverage, where they filmed me speaking — I mean, he totally didn’t need to do that,” Welling said. “We laughed a lot; he was very funny, and it got to the point where he was being told to leave. And he wouldn’t leave! His nurse was like, ‘If you don’t leave, I’m going to call the police, and I’m going to take you out of here.’ And he turned to me, and he goes, ‘They’re always telling me what to do,’ which is really funny, just considering the whole situation.” In “Smallville” lore, Clark landed on Earth as a toddler from the planet Krypton during a meteor shower that took a toll on the town, and he had super-strength, super-speed, X-ray vision, and was growing into all the abilities we associate with the character of Superman. The meteor rocks also infected Smallville and its population, which gave the show its engine for the case-of-the week format of its early seasons — and brought in a lot of guest stars, one of whom was Amy Adams in Season 1. Dan Doperalski for Variety Welling picked Brian Austin Green as his favorite (“because I watched ‘Beverly Hills, 90210’”), and Rosenbaum selected Adams “because it’s memorable and she became a big movie star, and she was really cool,” writing her name in cursive on the game’s whiteboard. “That’s respect,” Welling told Rosenbaum. “You’re an elegant man, Michael.” “TalkVille” has re-familiarized them with the show, so they had no problem remembering Adams’ episode. “‘Crave’ — she was a girl who craved to get thinner, right?” Rosenbaum asked. Welling replied, “She took kryptonite to get skinnier. And she took it too far.” Rosenbaum: “Yeah. She devoured people.” As the show’s central character, Welling appeared in every episode of “Smallville.” But Rosenbaum left after Season 7, following a contract dispute with Warner Bros. Television, the show’s producer. “I mean, do I get into it?” Rosenbaum wondered, looking to Welling, who then backed him up. “There’s a point in the show where the actor’s contract comes up for renewal, and the idea is that, based on the success of the show, the contract will be increased,” Welling said. “And that wasn’t happening.” Rosenbaum said he was already itching to do other things when the impasse occurred. “It was like, ‘Hey, we want you to come back for three years — we want you to sign a three-year deal, and give you no increase in pay,’” he recalled. “And anybody who works in any business, it’s like, ‘Oh, I’m an integral part of this show, or this business,’ or whether you work at Kmart or whatever. And you’re like, ‘I’m part of the success, and don’t I need to get rewarded?’ So I said, ‘Yeah, no thanks.’ And that was it.” Dan Doperalski for Variety Rosenbaum did return for the “Smallville” series finale, though, which aired on May 11, 2011 — with a full head of hair they had to cover with a bald cap. (He shaved his head to play Lex for the seven seasons he was on the show.) He’d called the then-showrunners Brian Peterson and Kelly Souders (Gough and Millar had also left after the seventh season) to say he wanted to come back one last time. Rosenbaum remembered thinking to himself, “You should come back and wrap it up for the fans — I think the fans will love it. And I didn’t realize how much I would love it, and I’m glad I did it.” Lex was a last-minute addition, and they had Rosenbaum for only one day, so Peterson and Souders had to scramble to explain where Lex had been for all those years, filming one last scene in the Luthor Mansion. (Additionally, in a flash-forward, Lex becomes president, portending ominous showdowns between Lex and Clark far in the future.) For Rosenbaum, it was an emotional return. “I was in the makeup trailer with Natalie, our makeup artist, who was like a mother to me,” he said. “I go, ‘All right, well, that’s it!” And I gave her a hug, and I just go, ‘Oh man. Oh, shoot. Here I go!’ I just started crying, and she cried, and we hugged it out, and that was it. It was bittersweet.” Throughout “Smallville,” Gough and Millar had a “no flights, no tights” ethos about the character, which Welling felt so strongly about that he had it in his contract. “We toed the line a few times, don’t get me wrong, but they couldn’t do it without me saying, ‘All right, this one will be all right.’” But in the finale’s last shot, after he’s been alerted to yet another crisis, Clark bounds up to the Daily Planet rooftop. As he prepares to take off, he rips open his shirt — revealing the classic imagery of the Superman suit. Welling remembers it well. “We didn’t even do a rehearsal on it, because we didn’t want anyone to see it if it wasn’t right,” he said. He’d wanted assurance that there wouldn’t be a full suit, and the head of wardrobe told him, “No, no, no — it’s too expensive.” “We got to set that day, and they had given me just a T-shirt, with no sleeves to wear underneath the shirt. Because they didn’t have the money to put the suit on, and they weren’t going to see it anyway.” Welling had been inspired by the conclusion of Kiefer Sutherland’s “24,” when Jack Bauer goes on the run and says his final goodbyes to his closest colleagues. Welling pitched that idea to the writers, he said, because he liked the idea of it as an ending to Clark’s story. “We can’t go with him,” Welling said. “But he’s out there.” As they reflected on “Smallville,” both Welling and Rosenbaum said they wished they’d appreciated it more at the time. “You’re on a hit show, and you’re doing all these things,” Rosenbaum said. “And sometimes you should really enjoy it, and embrace it. And I did; I think we both did. But if I could go back and do it again, I would’ve just been like, ‘Remember, this is fun . We’re getting paid to do this!'” Welling feels the same way. “I didn’t really have anybody who I knew to be like, ‘Hey buddy, you know this is cool, right?’” On Rosenbaum’s popular podcast “Inside of You,” “we talk about mental health, facing adversity, loss, all those things,” he said. He thinks a number of its listeners are “Smallville” fans. “The fans have stood by me, I think, for almost everything we do,” he said, crediting Gough and Millar — who’ve gone on to, among other projects, create “Wednesday” for Netflix – for how good the show was, and for creating the “family atmosphere” among the cast and crew. “Al and Miles,” Rosenbaum said, “it came down to them, and they chose us.” “I mean, we’re lucky,” he added. “People are like, ‘Well, do you think you’ll ever do anything as big as “Smallville?”’ I’m like, ‘Probably not!’” “But we were on one of the biggest shows ever, and isn’t that enough? It’s always, ‘What’s next? What are you doing?’ It’s like, ‘Hey dude, I’m content. I’m happy. And we kicked some ass for a while.” ©CW Network/Courtesy Everett Collection Loading comments... title: Banijay CEO: We Need Scale to Compete With Big Tech
full_text: × Skip to main content Breaking News Netflix Film Head Dan Lin Out close By Etan Vlessing Plus Icon Etan Vlessing Canada Bureau Chief View All October 19, 2026 7:26am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Marco Bassetti, CEO, Banijay Entertainment Tyler Miller Banijay Entertainment CEO Marco Bassetti fittingly discussed creating an even bigger indie production and distribution colossus in once-imperial Rome on Monday. “We want to define ourselves as an entertainment company,” after adding distribution and sports assets to an established production powerhouse, UK-based Bassetti said on stage at the Westin Excelsior Hotel as he addressed a global business upended by consolidation and technological disruption. But while describing the super indie as “big,” Bassetti added that, against Silicon Valley competitors like Alphabet and Meta as they grow exponentially, Banijay has had to get bigger still. The move by Banijay to scale up follows earlier acquisitions, like Zodiak Media in 2015 and Endemol Shine in 2019 . Banijay, while enabling All3Media producers a bigger international footprint, has also extended and expanded its own reach into live events, sports and across social media with Little Dot Studios. “We are producers on a global scale, we have to be big. But if we want to define the market everywhere, we’re small,” Bassetti said of the paradox of a growing European entertainment giant still being dwarfed in a fast-changing global entertainment and media business driven by Silicon Valley innovations. His comments follow the international production giant completing mega-merger with fellow indie giant All3Media to create a new $8.5 billion super indie. Not surprisingly, Bassetti during his informal conversation discussed the benefits of scale in today’s international TV business. “Every time we have a tranformational deal, it’s much better to buy a company with proven success, instead of starting from scratch. Getting to market as short as possible is crucial to our strategy,” he argued. The new London-based production and distribution group brings together nearly 200 production companies and labels across 25 territories, including the companies that make and sell such shows as The Traitors , Big Brother , Survivor , MasterChef , Peaky Blinders and Black Mirror , some hundreds of thousands of hours of programming, and combined revenues of $8.5 billion. The enlarged giant amid continuing industry consolidation is seen as beneficial as broadcasters and streamers need hit TV content and original IP as production budgets shrink after the end fo the Peak TV era. Speaking of scale, Bassetti talked about the recent Paramount takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery and as a combined company is set to produce 30 feature films each year and 80 series of all types on some 20 different networks and streamers. “The latest one is the biggest one of all — $111 million billion dollars,” he said of the combined studio led by CEO David Ellison, who he considers a friend. “You have to look at how much you invest, and the return on investment,” Bassetti said of his mergers and acquisitions strategy. “if you’re good, it’s an advantage.” THR

title: Nathan Fielder Says Elizabeth Holmes Called Him From Prison Right Before ‘You Can See Everything’ Release to Tell Him Repeatedly: ‘I Trust You’
full_text: Oct 19, 2026 7:20am PT Nathan Fielder Says Elizabeth Holmes Called Him From Prison Right Before ‘You Can See Everything’ Release to Tell Him Repeatedly: ‘I Trust You’ By Zack Sharf Plus Icon Zack Sharf Digital News Director ZSharf Latest Nathan Fielder Says Elizabeth Holmes Called Him From Prison Right Before ‘You Can See Everything’ Release to Tell Him Repeatedly: ‘I Trust You’ 2 hours ago Elizabeth Holmes’ Partner Billy Evans Admits ‘She Looks Insane’ in ‘You Can See Everything’ Trailer but Defends Making the Doc: ‘Make Up Your Own Mind’ 3 days ago Ben Affleck Says Bullying ‘Digger’ Will Only Lead Studios to Make More ‘S—ty Homogenized Movies’: Don’t ‘Punish Movies That Take Risks’ 4 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Jc Olivera / Justin Sullivan Nathan Fielder revealed in a new interview with Wired magazine that Elizabeth Holmes called him from prison right before the theatrical release of his new documentary, “ You Can See Everything .” The call marked the first time the director and his documentary subject had spoken in half a year. Ex-Theranos CEO Holmes is currently in federal prison after being convicted for fraud. “She had not called me in over six months. I had not heard from her in any way… she asked how I was doing,” Fielder said about their conversation. “I asked her if she had seen any stuff about the film coming out and how she felt about it. She told me she had seen some stuff, but most things she just isn’t seeing, so she’s heard things, but she hasn’t really read anything. And then, at the end, she said to me – ‘I trust you.’ I said, ‘OK, thanks.’” Related Stories Taylor Swift's 'The Life of a Showgirl' Spends 15th Week at No. 1 on Albums Chart Olivia vs. Olivia: Predicting the Grammys' Album of the Year Contenders... and Why Rodrigo and Dean Are at the Front of the Race Fielder continued, “We talked about some other stuff. She talked about her kids, and then some updates that are not really my place to share. But then after that, she said again, at the end of the call— ‘I trust you.’ And I don’t know what she meant by that.” Popular on Variety “You Can See Everything,” directed by Fielder and “Primetime” helmer Lance Oppenheim, follows Holmes and her partner Billy Evans in their final weeks before Homes’ 11-year prison sentence begins. The filmmakers moved in with the couple 34 days before Holmes went to prison. Fielder told Wired that he got involved with the project after hearing that Holmes and Evans had tried and failed to pitch a documentary about them to A24, explaining: “Months later, I heard that that had happened. So I called A24 and said, ‘Well, could I meet her?’ That was the start of it all.” But why would Holmes allow Fielder to come into her home? That’s a question that still has Fielder puzzled considering his previous work, be it “Nathan for You” or “The Rehearsal,” should’ve made it clear to Holmes that bringing Fielder on board would not produce anything straightforward or conventional. “This is part of the mystery that, like, doesn’t make sense to me,” Fielder said. “I asked her that on, I think, one of the first days we shot. I still don’t fully understand it. That really messed with my head. Also, I got the sense very early that she hadn’t seen a lot, but she had seen some of what I did, and she had talked to people who had seen what I did. Billy had seen more. I think she found the clip that she said she saw funny. But you know, her relationship to that … to what’s funny? I don’t even know. She said her favorite movie is ‘Elf,’ the Will Ferrell movie.” Evans appeared on the “All-In” podcast the day before “You Can See Everything” opened in theaters and explained the couple’s rationale behind letting Fielder and Oppenheim into their home. Mainly, they wanted people to get to know Holmes up close and personal so they could decide for themselves if she is a bad person or not. “It was to have people see who she is,” Evans said. “I have gone through this consistent experience with the people who love me most, from my grandmother to my best friends. They’d hear I knew [Elizabeth Holmes] or I was falling for this person and now we’re going to have a kid… in the beginning, every single one of these people thought I was crazy. ‘Do you know who she is?’ I would tell them, ‘I understand why you feel that way but just meet her.’ And they would meet her and spend time with her and see her in a totally natural environment, like going on a hike or helping a friend. Every opinion of her would radically shift. That was the intention of the film. To help scale that up and allow other people to sit with her and make up their own minds.” The decision is backfiring for Holmes, however, since “You Can See Everything” is only amplifying the backlash against her. Even before the movie screened for press, A24 dropped a chilling teaser trailer that had many viewers disturbed by Holmes’ demeanor and claims that she did not do anything wrong at Theronos. The movie has since turned into a box office hit by grossing $15 million in its domestic debut, which is the biggest launch for a documentary in decades. “You Can See Everything” is now playing in theaters nationwide. title: Russell Brand Trial: Police Asked Accuser What She Was Wearing During Alleged Oral Rape in Bar Toilet

Leon Neal/Getty Images Russell Brand ‘s rape and sexual assault trial is in its second week at London’s Southwark Crown Court. As a reminder, the ex-presenter, actor and comedian is accused of three counts of rape, three charges of sexual assault and one allegation of indecent assault, with six women alleging crimes dating from 1999 to 2009. He denies all of the claims, which were presented in depth by lead prosecutor Riel Karmy-Jones last week. The first complainant gave evidence on Thursday , telling the court about her and Brand’s 1999 encounter in a Bournemouth hotel room: “He did rape me, he did push me on the bed. … He did pull my clothes off.” She said the experience left her feeling “dirty” and in fear that she was pregnant. Brand maintains the interaction was consensual. Related Stories Movies Edward Berger Talks Filmmaking in a Streaming Age: "The Movie Industry Needed Netflix to Wake Up" Business Netflix Earnings Preview: Not the Time to Chill On Monday, another complainant’s police interview played as Brand watched on and his wife, Laura Gallacher, sat in the public gallery. The accuser went into detail about meeting Brand at a bar in Soho, London, in 2004. He went on to star in the likes of St. Trinian’s and Forgetting Sarah Marshall but was best known at this time for presenting Big Brother ‘s spinoff show. According to Sky News , the complainant said Brand grabbed at her breasts after talking “for a minute max.” She said Brand took her arm and dragged her into the toilets close to where they were standing. Here, the court was shown a floor plan of the bar. She said Brand stood on the toilet seat. “It happened so fast,” said the complainant in the police interview. “He pulled me over and put his penis in my mouth.” The woman explained that she tried to resist but Brand said, “‘Don’t be a spoilsport,’ or something along those lines.” She became emotional as she spoke, according to Sky, imagining others asking her: “‘Why didn’t you bite him?’ I just froze. I didn’t know what to do.” She alleged Brand then “ejaculated into my mouth.” The accuser recalled banging on the locked toilet door to escape and says a man outside may have shouted to ask if everything was okay. Brand acted as if “nothing had happened” and said to her: “I guess we should swap numbers now,” according to the woman. She says she was steered into a car with Brand, still in “disbelief and shock.” While in the car, she realized Brand had his penis out, the complainant claimed. She alleges he said, “Come on and suck it.” She says she told him no, and that Brand “took no for an answer.” On what was going through her mind at the time of the alleged oral rape, the accuser reportedly said: “If I do this maybe he won’t try to rape me further. … He won’t try to invade my body. … I felt it was the lesser of two evils.” She described it as a “survival thing,” and remembered thinking: “Just do what he wants and get out of here, and then it’s done. … I closed my eyes and tried to not be there.” She didn’t come forward to the police because, said the woman, she “felt shame that someone could do that to me.” It was only in 2023, after seeing reports in the press around other allegations against Brand, that she decided to come forward. Sky News added that the police interview showed the officer probing the woman on what she was wearing during the attack. She told them: “It wouldn’t have been boobs hanging out. I don’t dress like that.” The complainant says she was “absolutely appalled” when her employer, MTV, later hired him to be a presenter. “Any time he was in the building, I just refused to go over or to any parties. If I knew where he was, I would just avoid,” she said. “I did see him in the distance a couple of times. He probably wouldn’t even recognize me. I’m just a face.” The woman was then cross-examined by Brand’s defense lawyer, Ian Winter, who asked her on Monday: “Can you explain why you didn’t tell a single human being until you rang the police in September 2023?” She maintains she did tell people that Brand had grabbed her breasts while standing at the bar. Winter responded: “I suggest you didn’t tell anyone.” The woman answers: “I don’t agree with your summation.” Sky says the defense then asked: “Why didn’t you slap his face?” She said: “I was completely shocked someone I’d be talking to for around 30 seconds would do that to me.” Winter suggested it would have been “perfectly easy” for her to “struggle” or “kick off” about the interaction. She disagreed, telling the courtroom that the bar had “cleared out” a little. “I was dragged [into the toilet] against my will,” she added. Brand has pleaded not guilty to all the charges. The trial could last up to six weeks. THR

title: Angry Golf Bros Tried to Ruin Heather McMahon. She Released a Hulu Special Instead
full_text: × Skip to main content Breaking News Netflix Film Head Dan Lin Out close By Mikey O'Connell Plus Icon Mikey O'Connell Senior Entertainment Editor View All October 19, 2026 7:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Heather McMahon Courtesy of For a brief moment in 2025, it seemed like Heather McMahon was about to be canceled — and over a sequence of events so preposterous that the comedian couldn’t have scripted it herself. Hired to emcee the first tee of the Ryder Cup, the annual tournament that’s meant to be a friendly battle between American and European golfers, she was struggling to win over her crowd: a rowdy, largely drunk, overwhelmingly male and decidedly American horde at the Long Island course. When they started chanting “fuck you, Rory,” a dig at Northern Irish golf star Rory McIlroy, McMahon saw an opportunity to ingratiate herself with her new audience. What she got was a minor international incident . Related Stories TV Everybody Needs to Calm Down -- Comedian Laura Ramoso Says She Can Help With That Business Bowen Yang and Matt Rogers' 'Las Culturistas' to Stream On Disney+, Hulu The tournament fired McMahon. Tensions between the two teams escalated. She issued a public apology to McIlroy, but it was too late. For 72 hours, she was the recipient of the golf subsection of the manosphere’s vitriol and threats. She says she fielded challenges to meet up for physical fights. When she returned from a brief social media blackout, she was relieved to see her feed had been cleansed. “Taylor Swift really saved my ass,” recalls McMahon. “It was so bad for three days, and then she dropped Life of a Showgirl. The entire news cycle had changed.” But the impact of her brief cancellation stuck with McMahon, most auspiciously in her new special. By a Thread , which dropped on Hulu over the weekend, opens with McMahon’s vivid retelling of the event and the ensuing fallout. She also tackles myriad other subjects, but it’s a hell of a way to open the show. Speaking during a recent of The Hollywood Reporter podcast I’m Having an Episode (listen tot he full episode on Spotify , Amazon Music , Apple ), she talked about the similarities between sexism in sports and comedy — and how her enthusiasm for Pitbull landed her a Guinness World Record. With all respect to the emotional toll this cost you … as reasons for being “canceled” go, this one is pretty cartoonish. It’s hilarious. It’s insane. For the first three days, a full 72 hours, it was very scary. I had grown men sending me personal messages, messaging my managers, my publicists, everybody. “Have Heather meet me outside of XYZ steakhouse in Atlanta. We’re ready to brawl.” It is insane what people will send from their personal accounts. Like, this is from Bill. He’s an accountant. I can see what firm he works at. What was scary was that I had never been in that sort of situation, specifically in a man’s world. My audience is strongly females and fab gays. They get me. Afterwards, of course, every single one of my buddies in comedy messaged me like, “This is gold. This is the best thing that could happen to you.” Once I had apologized, once we got over the hump, I was like, there’s so much here. Having been raised in a very golf-centric family myself, what struck me about your experience is how rowdy the tournament crowds have gotten. It’s like the dark side of Happy Gilmore . How do you see it? Golf is in a really weird space. I grew up playing golf. I was a golfer in high school. It’s in my blood. My husband and I go to The Masters every year. The Ryder Cup has always been known to be heavily competitive between Europe and America. But it’s always been in good fun? I think [having it in Long Island], the already the weird animosity that America was having to outsiders, I don’t think they were set up for success that year. And, I’ll fall on the sword. I did not help the cause. It’s just really wild. What does golf want to be? Is it all buttoned up like The Masters? Is it trying to be Happy Gilmore? I do think golf needed like shake off the cobwebs, quit being as stuffy, but it doesn’t know where it wants to go. Has this has this experience changed your relationship golf? Yes and no. Golf has had some real moments recently. The Calloway situation! Who the fuck signed off on this shit? [ Calloway partnered with Good Good Golf on a commercial that depicted a man assaulting a woman .] You watch that and realize that this is the problem. I learned that men don’t want women in their spaces. You learn that a little bit in comedy, too. We’re already having to like elbow our way into rooms and to get the respect that we deserve. But the sports world? I had so many sports reporters and women in the business reach out to me say, “This happens across every sport. We all deal with the craziness.” I’m not even shitting on golf, because I’m still a huge fan, but I did just learn like I don’t need to be put in those spaces. I can enjoy it and do my thing. I’m only going to LPGA events now. Like that’s what I want to focus on and and root for the girls. It put a bad taste in my mouth for the the manosphere in general. So you’re watching the LPGA. Did you watch Rory win the Masters this year? I went to the Masters and got to see him win again. I’m still a huge fan. It’s not the players. They’re doing their thing. It’s just this kind of weird environment with some of the the male fans these days. And again, I apologized, but I do think, had a male comedian been in my shoes, we would have never had this conversation. They wouldn’t have given a shit. Dudes being dudes. Set it on fire, man. In a much lighter arena, I would like to address your Pitbull affinity. I started dressing in drag as Pitbull like 10 years ago, on a whim one Halloween. I went around trick-or-treating with a bunch of my friends’ kids and they had no idea it was me for like the first hour and a half. They just thought some creepy guy was following them. Then I started doing impressions as him. By my first tour, people just knew that was my shtick. I love Pitbull. But how did you come play such a prominent role at this past summer’s largest recorded gathering of Baldies — the people who wear bald caps to Pitbull shows? This past summer I get a text from a Miami number, and it’s Armando [Pérez], the real Pitbull. He’s like, “Heather, I’ve seen all your stuff. I adore you. We have to have you be a part of this Guinness Book of World Records party in Hyde Park.” So I end up going to London, I’m in drag. I host this full countdown to the concert with two other guys. I think like 75,000 people came out, but the people actually there in time to be counted for the Guinness Record was around like 22,000. It was just incredible. Guinness sent me a plaque that’s like, “You were a part of it.” It was unreal. And I got to hang out with Armando. They say, “Don’t meet your heroes,” in this business. But meet Pitbull. THR

title: Entertainment 360, Griffin Gaming Launch HITpoint to Bring Characters, Stories to Film, TV
full_text: × Skip to main content Breaking News Netflix Film Head Dan Lin Out close By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All October 19, 2026 7:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Walton Goggins in 'Fallout.' Prime Video Game on! Talent management and production company Entertainment 360 ( Game of Thrones, Ripley , Stick ), based in Century City, and Santa Monica-based gaming-centric venture capital firm Griffin Gaming Partners have teamed up to launch HITpoint Entertainment, a new company “dedicated to bringing the characters, worlds, and stories of video games to film and television.” HITpoint brings together the talent and production expertise of Entertainment 360 with Griffin Gaming ‘s relationships in the sector. Griffin has more than $1.6 billion in assets under management with its investments across the video game industry and adjacent spaces. Earlier this year , Griffin launched a fund for independent gaming titles with Hollywood potential. Both companies have experience at the intersection of gaming and Hollywood. Entertainment 360 clients are writing and starring in the upcoming The Legend of Zelda film, and the firm is also producing a recently unveiled an adaptation deal with Universal for an Atari property that wasn’t immediately disclosed. And Peter Levin , co-founder and managing director of Griffin Gaming, played a key role in bringing Fallout to the screen. “HITpoint will source, develop, package, and produce adaptations across the full range of genres represented in gaming – from action, horror, and high-concept spectacle to comedy, romance, and coming-of-age stories,” the partners said. The new company recognizes how core gaming has become in the entertainment landscape, with more than 3.7 billion people worldwide estimated to be actively playing video games. “Gen Z, which accounted for nearly 40 percent of North American moviegoers last year, ranks gaming as its favorite form of entertainment,” the partners also highlighted. Recent hit screen adaptations of games include A Minecraft Movie , Amazon’s Fallout series and HBO’s The Last of Us . They have “demonstrated the enormous potential of gaming IP across both theaters and streaming,” Griffin and Entertainment 360 said. “HITpoint will combine Griffin’s relationships with game developers and publishers with Entertainment 360’s producing track record on IP-driven franchises, including Game of Thrones. In addition to providing opportunities for the firm’s clients, the new venture will mine relationships across the broader creative community, pairing each property with the filmmakers, talent, and studio partners best suited to bring it to the screen.” The new company wants to pursue both established hit franchises and fast-growing independent games, drawing in part on Griffin’s new indie game fund to identify breakout titles and creators. “Video games represent one of the most exciting sources of stories and characters for film and television, but adapting them successfully requires a real understanding of the creativity and passion developers bring to their work,” said Levin. “Griffin has spent many years building trusted relationships across the gaming community, from major publishers to the independent studios we support. We see this vehicle as a differentiating resource for our 100+ portfolio companies, our strategic partners as well as the gaming ecosystem writ large. I couldn’t be more excited to partner with the team at Entertainment 360 and give fans new ways to experience the stories they already love.” “For younger audiences, games aren’t a side interest. They are where many of their favorite characters, stories, and worlds live,” said Entertainment 360, which was founded in 2002 and received a strategic minority investment from private equity firm Carlyle in 2025, allowing it to invest in its business. “There has long been an infrastructure in Hollywood for discovering books and other underlying material early. HITpoint brings that same focus to gaming. Together with Griffin, we can identify compelling IP at an early stage, bring it into a development environment, and pair it with filmmakers who genuinely understand the material and what makes it special.” Dedicated hires to manage HITpoint will be unveiled at a later stage. Respect for the source material will be central to HITpoint’s culture and business approach. “The company will keep game creators closely involved from initial development through production, aligning incentives while giving them direct access to leading writers, filmmakers, actors, and producing partners,” the partners highlighted. title: Locarno Golden Leopard Winner Sho Miyake Gets First North American Retrospective, 14-City Tour (EXCLUSIVE)
full_text: Oct 19, 2026 7:00am PT Locarno Golden Leopard Winner Sho Miyake Gets First North American Retrospective, 14-City Tour (EXCLUSIVE) By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest Locarno Golden Leopard Winner Sho Miyake Gets First North American Retrospective, 14-City Tour (EXCLUSIVE) 2 hours ago Ju Ji-hoon, Choo Young-woo Return for Netflix’s ‘The Trauma Code: Heroes on Call’ Seasons 2 and 3 6 hours ago Selena Gomez Reveals Vaping Nicotine Changed Her Voice: ‘It’s Not Worth It’ 6 hours ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Bitters End Japanese director Sho Miyake , whose “Two Seasons, Two Strangers” won the Golden Leopard at Locarno in 2025, will get his first North American retrospective at New York’s Metrograph from Nov. 7–17. It is one stop on a Japan Foundation tour of 14 cities in eight countries. The Metrograph program, titled “Unspoken Gestures: The Films of Sho Miyake,” is co-organized and presented by the Japan Foundation. Miyake will attend in person over the opening weekend, and select encore screenings will follow the main run. Related Stories Olivia vs. Olivia: Predicting the Grammys' Album of the Year Contenders... and Why Rodrigo and Dean Are at the Front of the Race Taylor Swift Spends Her 100th Week at No. 1 on the Billboard 200, as 'Life of a Showgirl' Stays on Top in Week 2 of 'Encore' Rebound The series brings together eight of Miyake’s own titles. They include his 2012 debut feature “Playback,” which premiered at Locarno, and “The Cockpit” (2014), a 64-minute film that watches producer-rapper OMSB and his collaborator Bim make a track in a small suburban Tokyo apartment. “And Your Bird Can Sing” (2018) screens with the 2016 short “August 8th,” and “Two Seasons, Two Strangers” is paired with the 2016 short “Nagahama.” Boxing drama “Small, Slow but Steady” (2022) and “All the Long Nights” (2024) round out the lineup. Popular on Variety Miyake has also picked two films that influenced his work as carte blanche selections: David Elfick’s 1973 surf film “Crystal Voyager” and Aoyama Shinji’s 2007 drama “Sad Vacation,” the final part of Aoyama’s “Kitakyushu Saga,” starring Asano Tadanobu. He will introduce both on Nov. 8, after Q&As following “Small, Slow but Steady” and “Two Seasons, Two Strangers” the day before. “For a long time now, Sho Miyake has been one of international cinema’s best-kept secrets, each of his films landing quietly but forcefully amid the cacophony of contemporary film culture. With this retrospective, we’re giving the man a microphone and calling on New York audiences to attend the voice of an essential Japanese film artist,” said Metrograph programmer Edo Choi. The tour opens on Nov. 3 in Washington, D.C., where the Japan Information & Culture Center at the Embassy of Japan will screen “Two Seasons, Two Strangers” and Miyake will join the Q&A remotely. Oklahoma follows from Nov. 9–11, with screenings at the University of Oklahoma’s Meacham Auditorium in Norman and the Oklahoma City Museum of Art. Miyake will also teach a masterclass for a university screenwriting class that is closed to the public. Los Angeles hosts the program Nov. 13–15 at the Japan Foundation, Los Angeles, UCR Arts at the University of California, Riverside, and the American Cinematheque’s Los Feliz Theatre. The lineup there adds King Vidor’s “The Patsy” (1928) and Tony Scott’s “Deja Vu” (2006). Toronto runs Nov. 17–19 at TIFF Bell Lightbox, the Fox Theatre and Paradise Cinema, with Miyake’s 2010 film “Good for Nothing” and Jacques Demy’s “Bay of Angels” (1962) on the bill. In the new year, the tour heads to Paris, Toulouse, Rome, Turin, Madrid, Zurich, Cologne, London and Derby, and wraps in February 2027. Miyake will travel to every city except Washington. In a joint statement, Inoue Ryo and Rokkaku Akinaru of the Japan Foundation pointed to Miyake’s own description of a director’s job as “taking on the responsibility of creating images of humanity.” “We, too, are among the audience members who were once struck and moved by his gaze. We sincerely hope to bring that sense of wonder and emotion to as many viewers as possible in theaters around the world,” they said. Miyake made “Playback” while still in his mid-twenties. Murakami Jun plays an actor nearing 40 who wakes up on the way to a hometown wedding wearing his old school uniform. His friend Hamaguchi Ryusuke compared the film to “a modern-day reincarnation of [John Cassavetes’s] ‘Opening Night.’” “Small, Slow but Steady” stars Kishii Yukino and is drawn from the life of deaf boxer Ogasawara Keiko. “All the Long Nights,” adapted from Seo Maiko’s novel, pairs Matsumura Hokuto and Kamishiraishi Mone as co-workers who form a bond. “Two Seasons, Two Strangers” adapts two manga by Tsuge Yoshiharu and stars Kawai Yuumi, Takada Mansaku, Shim Eun-kyung and Tsutsumi Shinichi. title: Globo, Netflix Strike Biggest Licensing Deal Between the Two Companies, Led by Walter Salles’ Oscar Winner ‘I’m Still Here’ (EXCLUSIVE)
full_text: Oct 19, 2026 7:00am PT Globo, Netflix Strike Biggest Licensing Deal Between the Two Companies, Led by Walter Salles’ Oscar Winner ‘I’m Still Here’ (EXCLUSIVE) Kicking in from December, the deal sees 18 wide-ranging Globo titles, including International Emmy Winner 'India – A Love Story,' hitting Netflix in Brazil or worldwide By John Hopewell Plus Icon John Hopewell Chief International Correspondent john_hopewell Latest Globo, Netflix Strike Biggest Licensing Deal Between the Two Companies, Led by Walter Salles’ Oscar Winner ‘I’m Still Here’ (EXCLUSIVE) 2 hours ago YouTube’s Virtues, Industry Consolidation, Christie Brinkley and ‘Baywatch’: Trends and Themes From a Busy Mipcom 4 days ago ‘The Castle’ Shapes Up as Another Hit From ‘La Bola Negra’ Producer Movistar Plus 4 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Credit: Alile Dara Onawale - Globoplay When the going gets tough, the tough get together: Brazil’s Globo , Latin America’s biggest media company, has struck an 18-title licensing deal with Netflix , led by one jewel in Globo’s crown, Walter Salles ’ Academy Award winner “ I’m Still Here .” Kicking in from December, the agreement sees titles rolling out on Netflix through mid-2027. The wide-ranging deal also takes in “India – A Love Story,” created by Glória Perez, the doyenne of Brazilian telenovela writers, and directed by Marcos Schechtman, which won the 2009 International Emmy for Best Telenovela. Related Stories Taylor Swift Spends Her 100th Week at No. 1 on the Billboard 200, as 'Life of a Showgirl' Stays on Top in Week 2 of 'Encore' Rebound Todd Rundgren Slams Taylor Swift, Says She ‘Ruined Music’ and Is ‘the Apotheosis of Mediocrity’ Also in the mix is “Vitória,” directed by notable film-TV helmer Andrucha Waddington (“Under Pressure,” “Emergency 53”) and starring Academy Award nominee Fernanda Montenegro (“Central Station”) in a lauded central performance as an 80-year-old battling to expose a drug racket on Copacabana. Popular on Variety Rights details vary. Sold worldwide by Goodfellas in theatrical deals, “I’m Still Here” has been licensed just for Brazil. Netflix has closed the U.S. and Latin America, a telenovela heartland, on “India – A Love Story.” Created by Leandro Soares and directed by João Fonseca and Regis Faria, seven seasons of “Vai Que Cola,” Brazil’s biggest pay TV comedy series hits, running over 2013-26, has been acquired by Netflix in Brazil. “Vitória,” in contrast has been bought for the world. The Globo original productions will be made available on Netflix, dubbed and subtitled in multiple languages. The package is comprised by 14 films, three telenovelas and a series. “We hope this agreement is just the first step in a long partnership between two companies that share the ambition, creative craftsmanship and commitment to take Brazilian culture even further”, said Elisabetta Zenatti, VP of Content at Netflix Brazil. “It makes us proud to see interest in Brazilian productions growing across different markets,” said Pedro Garcia, Globo’s Director of Rights. “For decades, we have been dedicated to sharing the richness of our culture with the world. By combining that experience with Netflix’s global scale, we take another step toward bringing Brazilian creativity to new audiences, expanding the presence and strengthening the recognition of Brazilian film and television abroad.” Several broader market trends are also at work. “The deal is a reflection of a wider trend in streaming,” said Guy Bisson, Ampere Analysis executive director. “Licensing spend is growing while original production spend is flat,” he added. “Content owners can no longer afford to keep their own content in long windows of exclusivity or in perpetuity given the challenge of customer acquisition in a saturated market so we’re seeing more content enter the market again and windows shortening. Courtesy of Netflix Why Globo Is Important to Netflix? “Both companies say the move underscores the power of Brazilian content to entertain audiences around the world,” Globo and Netflix noted in a press statement Monday. Globoplay co-produced “I’m Still Here” and saw it gross a remarkable $36.5 million worldwide, racking up $17 million in box office gross outside Brazil, including $6.2 million for Sony Pictures Classics in the U.S. Globo announced at Mipcom that Globoplay Original “Red Blood,” a teen werewolf-vampire love triangle thriller, has sold at the BBC. Equally, Netflix has seen a surge in international audiences’ passion for Brazilian fiction, movie “Caramelo” reigning s Netflix No. 1 non-English film in the world over Oct. 6-19 last year. “Rulers of Fortune,” and “Radioactive Emergency,” also hit the Netflix Global No. 1, Non-English show spot, over Nov. 3-9, 2025 and March 23-29 this year. As a streaming service , Netflix reigns supreme in Latin America, where it has 63.8 million subscriptions forecast for 2026, which will increasing to 73.7 million by 2031, María Rúa Aguete, Head of Media and Entertainment at Omdia, announced at Mipcom. Brazil is said to have more Netflix subscribers than any other country in the world outside the U.S. at a time when international revenue growth is increasingly vital to Netflix’s fortunes. Globo can supply some of its drivers. It will have a Halloween 2027 premiere on the streamer. The order comes nine months after the project landed at Disney+ with a big script-to-series commitment . Afterlife with Archie comes from the same auspices as the CW’s Riverdale and Netflix’s Chilling Adventures of Sabrina : writer Aguirre-Sacasa, Greg Berlanti ‘s Berlanti Productions and Warner Bros. Television where Aguirre-Sacasa and Berlanti are under overall deals. When a supernatural spell from a certain teen-witch backfires, unleashing an army of the possessed dead upon Riverdale, Archie and his friends must fight to stay alive, testing the friendships, romances, and loyalties that have always held them together. Watch on Deadline Afterlife with Archie is executive produced by Aguirre-Sacasa and Jimmy Gibbons via Muckle Man; Greg Berlanti, Sarah Schechter, Leigh London Redman via Berlanti Productions; and Jon Goldwater via Archie Comics Studios. “ Afterlife with Archie has always been about more than just zombies — it’s about the friendships, loyalty and humanity that make Riverdale worth fighting for,” said Ayo Davis, president, Disney Kids & Family. “Roberto, Greg, Sarah and Jon have such a deep appreciation for these characters, and they’ve built something that’s equal parts thrilling and heartfelt. Fans are going to fall hard for this new version of the gang … and maybe scream a little too.” This is Aguirre-Sacasa, Berlanti Prods. and Warner Bros. TV’s third live-action Archie Comics series adaptation — and the first to launch on the outlet it was originally sold to. Riverdale was initially set up at Fox before moving to the CW, Chilling Adventures of Sabrina started at the CW before relocating to Netflix. Riverdale spawned a short-lived spinoff series on the CW, Katy Keene. Afterlife with Archie also marks Warner Bros. TV’s first series for Disney+, which has been increasingly opening up its slate to outside studios. “The world of ‘Archie’ and Riverdale is the gift that keeps on giving,” said Channing Dungey, Chairman and CEO, Warner Bros. Television Group and WBD US Networks. “To bring Roberto Aguirre-Sacasa’s incredible story to life with our partners at Berlanti Productions, ArchieComics and Disney+ is a thrill for all of us at WBTVG.” Aguirre-Sacasa, a film, TV and comic book writer, had written Archie Comics’ two best-selling horror series, Afterlife With Archie and Chilling Adventures Of Sabrina , when he was named the publisher’s Chief Creative Officer in March 2014. Twelve years later, he continues in his role while also expanding his TV footprint — and the Archie TV universe which launched with the 2017 Riverdale. “This was the comic book that started it all. Before there was a Riverdale, before there was a Chilling Adventures of Sabrina, there was Afterlife with Archie , which I collaborated on with the best horror artist in the business, Francesco Francavilla,” Aguirre-Sacasa said. “Getting to turn Afterlife into a TV series for the amazing team at Disney+ with our incredible partners at Berlanti Productions, WB and, of course, Jon (Goldwater) and his Archie family is truly a full-circle moment — and the ultimate dream project for me. Time to say a prayer for Archie, Betty, Veronica and the whole gang, ‘cause THE ZOMBIES ARE COMING!!!!” Berlanti Prods. and WBTV also have the upcoming Scooby-Doo! live-action series at Netflix, the HBO drama pilot How To Survive Without Me , Stillwater , based on the Skybound comic books, which has a series commitment at Amazon , as well as All American , which just launched its eighth and final season on the CW. “We are so happy to reunite with Roberto on this exciting series that takes us back into the Riverdale world that we so love, and we are thankful to Disney+ and WBTV for giving us the opportunity to revisit some of our favorite characters in a unique and thrilling way,” Berlanti and Schechter said. “A special thank you to Jon Goldwater for letting us continue to play within the beloved ‘Archie’ universe and trusting us to bring Archie’s various stories to life.” Aguirre-Sacasa is repped by WME and Sloane, Offer, Weber & Dern. Berlanti is repped by CAA and Felker McGinnis & Ryan. Schechter and Goldwater are repped by CAA.
